A letter containing the correct and blameless faith, sent by the most blessed Pope Thomas, patriarch of Jerusalem, to the heretics in Armenia. It was dictated in Arabic by Theodore, surnamed Abu Qurrah, bishop of Harran, and translated by Michael, the least of presbyters and synkellos of the apostolic throne of Jerusalem, through whom it was also sent. A letter containing [?]

[?] Of Theodore, surnamed Abu Qurrah, bishop of Harran. [?] That we have five enemies, from which the Saviour redeemed [us]. In the form of question and answer. A. We have five deadly enemies, from which Christ, by becoming man, redeemed us. B. I would gladly learn who they are and how he redeemed us from each, and I earnestly ask you to explain. A. Since you are eager to learn, I will explain what you ask as well as I am able [?]. But first tell me what I ask you.

A. Do you say that the God who is over all does or declares [?] anything in vain and at random? B. How could it be pious to say this of God, when it cannot be said even of people who have sound judgment and [?]? A. When, then, he pronounced against the man who had transgressed his commandment, "You are earth, and to earth you shall return," in keeping with his earlier warning to him, "On the day you eat of" what was forbidden (clearly the tree) "you shall surely die," how could he annul his own sentence unless some other reason had arisen that justly set it aside? If you saw a judge pass a judgment today and then cancel it tomorrow, would you not think him mad? How, then, could God overturn his first judgment and sentence? B. Tell me how, for I cannot see it. A. What is the cause of the condemnation to death? B. Disobedience, obviously. A. Just as through the disobedience of the one man

Adam death entered the world and so passed to all human beings, so also through the obedience of the one man, the second Adam, Christ, death will reasonably be abolished and life brought in in its place. B. But before Christ, did not Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses and Enoch obey God and please him [?]? A. They are indeed said to have pleased God, but only in comparison with the rest of humankind. Strictly speaking, and in every respect, no one has been without any taste of sin except Christ. And every sin, even the slightest, brings death. So, as far as the principle of justice is concerned, once Christ had rendered perfect obedience and had repelled all the assaults of the devil in the struggle in the wilderness, he dissolved death and through his own obedience brought in life in its place. B. Then what further need was there for death on the cross, since the condemnation to death had been dissolved? A. But the devil's charge against us would have remained. Or do you not know that we became subject to him, because we disobeyed God and obeyed him? What would it have mattered to him, so to speak, if death were overturned while his tyranny and authority [?] remained? Indeed he would have rejoiced all the more, as over immortal [?]

B. I would like to learn in what way we became slaves of the devil. A. When God formed man in the beginning, he made him strong and invincible. The devil, unable to overcome him by force but clever at doing harm, contrived and schemed against him until, through his voluntary disobedience, he stripped him of the grace that strengthened him, having [ensnared] [?] him through pleasure. And so, once man had been weakened, the devil prevailed over him and easily led him and his descendants into every pleasure, sin and disobedience. Thereafter God, since man had scorned his commandment, run over to the enemy and [?], justly allowed him to be tyrannized by the enemy. (For whomever one obeys, to him one shows oneself a slave, as the Apostle says: "You are slaves of the one you obey.") So man, though he was free, sold himself to pleasure and to the

B. And how is it that man, having repented after the sin, could not recall himself and shake off the devil's yoke? A. Because selling ourselves is in our power, but freeing ourselves after the sale and the enslavement is not. Nor do we say that the devil became our lord in the sense of ruling us entirely by force, but that we were weakened through sin and from then on, like sick people, became easy prey for the devil, readily [?] led into his sins and pleasures. For just as,

if an enemy contrives to make his foe drink a poison that makes him ill, so that once he has become weak he may then easily overcome him, so the devil enticed man by means of the forbidden food and, once he had become weak, seized him. So he held us in subjection. And [so we would have remained] had not Christ baited our adversary until he killed him unjustly; and through that unjust killing Christ took both the devil himself and all the slaves subject to him. In this way Christ's own just dealing rescued us from slavery to the devil, and also, so to speak, shook death off from us. For Satan held us as those who had obeyed him. B. I would like to learn this more clearly through an illustration. A. Suppose there is a king in some country who has slaves. Suppose a river surrounds this country, and beyond the river lies a planted garden bearing beautiful and delightful fruit. Suppose the king forbids all his slaves to cross the river to that garden. But one of those slaves, charmed by the sight of those fruits and his desire for them, slackened by his own appetite, and senselessly overcome, [disregards] the master's command and crosses the river to sate his desire. And suppose he not only does this, but also deceives the rest of his fellow slaves, enticing them with the pleasure of the fruits he shows them to disobey their common master, cross the river and come under his hand. Then suppose that this author of evil tyrannizes and oppresses these fellow slaves. The oppressed cry out to their own master and call on him to deliver them from the evils that beset them. Then the most holy king, taking pity on them, sends his own son, clothed in the garb of the slaves and made like them in every respect. He comes into their midst and walks along the banks of the river. Seeing him, and supposing him to be one of the slaves, the tyrant, the author of evil, urges him as usual with the pleasures of the fruits to cross the river and come under him. But when he does not obey, and firmly rejects his urgings, the tyrant, burning with jealousy and envy, crosses the river and kills the king's son. The king then seizes him and questions him, saying: "Tell me, you utterly wicked one: when you persuaded the other slaves to disobey me, their natural master, and cross over to you, did I snatch them from your hands and from your slavery, since they had willingly submitted to you? I did not, though I had the power and strength to do so; for I did not wish to falsify justice. But this one, who is my son and did not yield in the least to your enticements, why did you kill him [Note: Thus in B; read ὑποτοπάσας ("supposing").]

and put him to death unjustly? Since then [?] of one [drop] of the royal blood [?] he rescued [us] on a just principle, and not simply by using might and power." B. Enough has been said about this. Now tell me the five enemies from which Christ redeemed us. A. Death, the devil, the curse and condemnation of the law, sin, and Hades. B. About death you have said that it was dissolved through Christ's obedience, and likewise how he delivered us from the devil's dominion. Now tell me how he redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. A. Remember what was said earlier in my discourse: that since we have transgressed God's law ten thousand times, we deserve to die ten thousand times. Tell me—I asked you this first in the case of Adam—does God do anything in vain and at random? B. Heaven forbid! A. Suppose someone owed another thousands of gold coins which he could not pay, and the creditor did not want to demand the amount of gold from him, yet for no reason wrote out a bond against him, took him and put him in prison, and grieved and afflicted him in every way, though, as I said, he did not want to receive the sum from him, and afterwards released him without exacting it [?]. Would we not consider such a person foolish? B. Of course. A. If, then, God did not want to demand of us the requirements of the law, why did he write it against us? But it is not so—heaven forbid! [For] God is not frivolous, as though playing games; rather, in his just judgment he demanded of us everything written in the law. And since we were unable to pay, our Master Christ paid on our behalf, took upon himself the curse and condemnation that we owed, and accepted it willingly. What we ought to have suffered, he suffered himself. He was scourged, and [?], and slapped, and buffeted, and [?] … to annul and abolish [his own] justice.

Yet it is not itself a substance [in this sense], nor a nature; for not all the things that are equal under it are consubstantial and of the same nature, as is evident to everyone. Look: a man, a pomegranate and a stone are equal under this substance, for each of them receives both the name and the definition of substance; yet they are neither consubstantial nor of the same nature. It is agreed, then, that the term "substance" is used in two ways, the logical and the philosophical. To put it simply, every philosophical term, as soon as it is spoken, lets the hearer think of some existing thing in a determinate way—once any ambiguity has, of course, been removed from it—so that nothing else can be understood from it except the thing defined. For example, if someone says the word "man", the hearer at once thinks of a defined thing, that is, a rational, mortal animal, capable of mind and knowledge, and can grasp nothing else from the word "man" except the thing defined. But every term spoken as a logical term does not let the hearer think of any existing thing except indeterminately, since it is applied to many different things. For example, the word "species", being a logical term, ranges widely and applies to man, horse, ox, gold, circle, grammar and a great many other differing things; so it does not allow the hearer to understand anything determinate. Likewise, if someone says the name "Paul", cleared of ambiguity, it at once lets one think of, say, the great Apostle, once the persecutor of the Church, together with the other properties that characterize the person meant, which could never belong to anyone else. if you say that Peter, Paul and John are three men, you will have counted what you did not propose to subject to number. For we said before that "man" is none of these. And if you say that these very individuals are three [men], you will count each of them as three, so that the three are multiplied into nine, which is impossible. Hence we must bring in the logical term that fits each of them, namely "hypostasis", "individual" or "person". Under this term those proposed for counting will be subjected to number, and they are called three hypostases, or individuals, or persons. In this very way it is shown that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not three gods, even though each of them is perfect God—just as each of those men is a perfect man, yet they are not called three men. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, then, are three hypostases, just as those men are. From this we shall clearly know that Christ must be confessed to be one hypostasis in two natures. For Christ is the eternal Son of God made flesh, that is, the one hypostasis of the Holy Trinity made flesh; and this hypostasis, namely the eternal Son, is himself God and man together. So if you wish to count God and man, who are the eternal God, that is, the one hypostasis, you cannot call them two hypostases. For neither the word "God" nor the word "man" signifies a hypostasis. A hypostasis is predicated of nothing at all, so neither of these is a hypostasis. Nor is it right to call God and man two genera, since each genus is predicated of [species] proper to it [?], while neither of these is predicated of anything proper to it [?]. Nor is it fitting to call them two species, for each species is ranked under a genus; but God will not be subordinated to a genus, as man is. It is therefore more proper to count them as two natures and two substances, for each of them is both a nature and a substance for the things of which it is predicated. None of the things under either of them has constitutive differences, that is, differences of substance and nature, from the others, so each is the nature and substance of the things of which it is predicated. It has been shown in many ways, therefore, that a hypostasis is not a nature, nor indeed the logical substance that ranges widely in every way, as a nature does [?]. And Orthodoxy says that the nature is neither one hypostasis of those of which it is predicated, nor all the hypostases that may be under it. For example, the Godhead, that is, God, is not the Father; for if it were the Father, the Son would certainly not be God. For [?]

But if we say that the [Son] and his own body are not two things, they retort, saying: "If these are not two things, how can you say that Christ is two natures?" To them we shall say: We do not count the eternal Son together with his own body so as to call them two things. The body of the eternal Son is hypostatic to him, and in a certain way it perfects him insofar as he is man. Every thing that perfects another thing does so either as genus, or as difference, or as nature (that is, essence), or as something hypostatic, and so it belongs to that other thing, perfecting it and giving it subsistence. Since, then, the body of the eternal Son is hypostatic, it is in no way counted together with him, even though it is not said to perfect him simply, that is, in the proper sense. But this is no reason to deny that two natures are spoken of in Christ. For when we, the orthodox, speak of two natures, we do not count the eternal Son together with his own hypostatic body. Rather, we count the Godhead and the manhood as two natures. Perhaps someone thinking about this will say: "Is not the Master's manhood, then, simply his own ensouled and rational body?" We shall reply to him that it is not. For the manhood of Christ is the manhood of all of us human beings, whereas his ensouled and rational body is his alone, in a distinctive way. If anyone should contend against this, he will fall into one absurdity or the other. Either he will be compelled to say that Christ's manhood is not the manhood of all of us, and so to introduce many manhoods, or he will have to say that the body of the [eternal] Son is the body of each one of us human beings. And in that case let such a person eat the body of Christ and the body of some robber or atheist alike. [?]
