B. Enough has been said about this. But tell me [?] the five enemies from whom Christ redeemed us.
A. Death, the devil, the curse and condemnation of the law, sin, and Hades.
B. You have said that death was undone through Christ's obedience, and likewise how he delivered us from the devil's dominion. Now explain how he bought us out of the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.
A. Remember what I said earlier: we have transgressed God's law ten thousand times, so we deserve to die ten thousand times. Tell me, as I first asked you concerning Adam: does God do anything in vain and at random?
B. Certainly not.
A. Suppose someone owed another man thousands of coins and was unable to repay them. Suppose the creditor did not wish to demand the amount of the [?] debt from him, yet wrote a bond against him for no purpose, took him, put him in prison and afflicted him in every way, not wishing, as I said, to receive the amount from him, and afterwards, when asked, released him. Do we not regard such a person as acting in vain?
B. Of course.
A. If, then, God did not wish to demand from us what the law requires, why did he write it against us? But it is not so, God forbid! God is not meddlesome, nor does he act as if he were playing. In his righteous judgment he demanded everything written in the law. And since we were unable to pay, Christ our Master paid on our behalf. He took the curse and condemnation owed by us and willingly accepted it. What we ought to have suffered, he himself suffered. He was scourged and bound [?], slapped and struck, crucified, and died for us. And although, as [?], through his obedience to undo [?] ... but out of abundance, so that he might deliver us both from the devil and from the curse of the law [?] of God's righteous judgment, he died for us. In this way God could have mercy on us without annulling and abolishing his justice, but [?]

... carried about, is shown indefinitely in the case of Paul and Peter and this horse and [?] the white and this circle, and the rest likewise, which are not divided at all, that is, which are predicated of others. From this, then, it is clear that the name "nature" and "essence," taken logically, and "hypostasis" belong to those terms that are carried about and applied indefinitely to many, that is, to logical terms, just like the names "species" and "individual," as we have shown. For the name "nature" [?] is applied to man, horse, gold and the rest, being carried about widely, just like the name "species." In the same way the name "hypostasis" is applied to Peter, Paul, this horse and this ox, as is "individual."
This plainly exposes the ignorance of the deranged heretic Severus. For he says: "Paul is a hypostasis and man is a nature; just as Paul is said to be man, so let hypostasis also be said to be nature." But we shall overturn the senseless man's folly with this reply: By the method you have put forward, you witless man, since Paul is an individual and man is a species, then just as you say that Paul is man, say also that the individual is a species. Then, just as you give Paul the definition and name of man, you will likewise give the individual the definition and name of species. And so you will say that the individual is "what is predicated of many things differing in number, in answer to the question 'what is it?'" That is the height of folly, and it suits him above all other heretics. Again, you say that Paul is an essence, which is the most generic genus, and you give Paul the definition of essence, namely "a self-subsistent thing that needs nothing else for its existence." In the same way, let the individual also be called the most generic genus, and give the individual the definition and name of the most generic genus, namely "that above which there is no higher genus, and which is always a genus." But who would accept this, except someone wholly estranged from divine grace? From all this, anyone with sense must conclude that hypostasis is not nature. Nor is it essence, which, like nature, is carried about and ranges in every way, that is, logically [?]. For all things of the same nature are certainly also of the same essence, and conversely all things that differ in essence [differ in nature], so that nature and essence are the same.
One must know that things are not counted under philosophical names by way of combination, but some [names] apply to them [?]. For instance, if we wished to count Peter, [Paul] and John, we do not say [?] "men," since each of them is a man, but none of them is "men." For the lesser are not predicated of the greater, but the greater of the lesser [?]. You would no longer say that man is [Peter] [?], but you would say that [Peter] is man. If, then,

[?] ... the predication does not convert, as is clear to everyone: the Father is God, but God is not in every case the Father. And the Son is God, and likewise the Holy Spirit. So God is not any one of these three. Nor are all three together God. For if God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, [then] whatever is God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. But each of these, being perfect God, is not [?] the three. This is plain and evident, at least to those who have sense. Yet the Severians, those utterly senseless heretics, put forward certain heretical problems against us orthodox. Let us bring them into the open and, with God's help, refute them as rotten and [?].
These vain-minded people will say to us: "If you say that God is not these three, then tell us: is God a thing, or not?" When we answer that God is a thing, they ask again: "And are the three hypostases not three things?" When we agree that these too are things, they draw their conclusion against us: "Then by your account God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit are counted as four things. So you are convicted of denying the Trinity and introducing a tetrad." But we answer them: Not knowing the true path of demonstration, you people, you utter these fallacies. You do not know that every thing that perfects another thing is not counted together with the thing it perfects. For example, the [gold] of a coin is not the coin itself, for gold, insofar as it is gold, does not have the coin's stamp. Now the gold is a thing, and the coin in turn is another thing. Yet the gold, though it is a thing, [is not] counted together with the coin. So these are not called two things, and they should not even be joined with the conjunction "and." It is crude and very ignorant to say "coin and gold." The same is to be understood of Paul and his own body. Paul is not his body, nor is the body Paul. [Paul] is a thing, and the body too is a thing, but Paul is not counted together with his own

body so that the two are two things. Why? Because his own body perfects Paul. [So too the Godhead,] [?] which is predicated of the hypostases, is not counted together with the three hypostases so that it and they are four things, as the heretics say in their dreams. The heretics put forward another problem of this kind against orthodoxy. They say: "Do you say that the eternal Son is a thing, or not?" When we say that he is a thing, they ask again: "And the ensouled and rational body of the eternal Son, do you not say that it is a thing?" When we agree that this too is a thing, they immediately conclude against us: "Then you count the eternal Son together with his own body." They say this so as to bind us on both sides, as far as they can, with straps of spider's web, and either cast us into absurd blasphemy or draw us over to their own way of thinking. For if we call the eternal Son and his ensouled and rational body two things, they will at once condemn us for setting four things on the lofty throne of the Godhead, which is a denial of the Trinity. But if we say that the Son and his own body are not two things, they retort, saying: "If these are not two things, how can you say that Christ is two natures?" To them we shall say: We do not count the eternal Son together with his own body so as to call them two things. The body of the eternal Son is hypostatic to him, and in a certain way it perfects him insofar as he is man. Every thing that perfects another thing does so either as genus, or as difference, or as nature (that is, essence), or as something hypostatic, and so it belongs to that other thing, perfecting it and giving it subsistence. Since, then, the body of the eternal Son is hypostatic, it is in no way counted together with him, even though it is not said to perfect him simply, that is, in the proper sense. But this is no reason to deny that two natures are spoken of in Christ. For when we, the orthodox, speak of two natures, we do not count the eternal Son together with his own hypostatic body. Rather, we count the Godhead and the manhood as two natures. Perhaps someone thinking about this will say: "Is not the Master's manhood, then, simply his own ensouled and rational body?" We shall reply to him that it is not. For the manhood of Christ is the manhood of all of us human beings, whereas his ensouled and rational body is his alone, in a distinctive way. If anyone should contend against this, he will fall into one absurdity or the other. Either he will be compelled to say that Christ's manhood is not the manhood of all of us, and so to introduce many manhoods, or he will have to say that the body of the [eternal] Son is the body of each one of us human beings. And in that case let such a person eat the body of Christ and the body of some robber or atheist alike. [?] read "therefore" [?] the Godhead perfects each one [?].

And again, if they say that Christ's manhood is not our manhood, they will be forced to say that Christ's Godhead is not that of the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so to introduce three godheads. That is complete apostasy from Christianity. But if he says the other thing, the utterly shameful consequence we mentioned earlier is enough to refute whoever asserts it.
It must be known that the holy Fathers sometimes say that the eternal Son was begotten from the Father, and sometimes from the essence of the Father. We, the orthodox, say that the Father's essence is not the Father himself but something besides the Father. So they immediately broadcast against us that we have been caught saying the Son was born from two things, and that the Father is counted together with his own essence. How we answer them has already been shown in what was said before. When we answer them thus, the deranged people will say: "Even if we grant that this is as you have said, you are still forced to say that the Son was not born from the same thing." To these senseless people we shall reply, to put them to shame: Truly you are in error, you wretches, because you do not know the [meaning] [?] of what is said. We are not forced to say what you suppose. Even if the Father is one thing and the Father's essence another, nevertheless when we say that the Son was begotten from the essence of the Father, or from the Father, we mean that he was born from the same thing, not from one thing and another, God forbid! When you say, "I weighed the gold of the coin," you are saying that the gold itself was placed on the scale. And again, when you say, "I weighed the coin," you are saying that the gold is weighed, for the stamp of the coin is not weighed, as everyone knows. In the same way, even if we say that the Son was begotten from the Father's essence, we are not forced to say that he was born from two things, but from one and the same thing. So orthodoxy always proves victorious and carries off the prizes of victory against the heretics.
Again they spring a question on us, saying: "When the eternal Son became incarnate, did he assume a common thing [or a particular one]?" If we should say that he assumed a particular thing, we would be led to speak of two hypostases in Christ, in the same way that we speak of two natures. Then we would fall in with the most abominable thinking of the Nestorians, for with them hypostasis is the particular thing. Or else we would have to deny two natures in Christ altogether, just as we deny two hypostases, and from that

we would be driven to be called Severians, saying that Christ is one nature in the same way that we say he is one hypostasis. That is full of destruction for the soul. But if we say that the Son assumed a common thing, they immediately attack us, saying: "Then how was the Son incarnated, having assumed this? For it is impossible for something incorporeal to become embodied by being united to something incorporeal." Let us answer them: You have [not] understood, you people, the meaning of the philosophers who said that the common is incorporeal. For they say that every genus and species is incorporeal, and they also say that body itself, which is divided from the highest essence called the most generic genus, is incorporeal. Therefore one must know that, according to the philosophers, the name "incorporeal" is used equivocally and indefinitely. To put it comprehensively, they call incorporeal matter and form (from which bodies come), color, every shape (that is, every quality), the soul, the angels, and the divine itself. These do not all have one and the same nature; their natures are many and different. This clearly confirms that the name "incorporeal" is used equivocally and indefinitely, signifying many things and applied to things that differ in nature. Body, then, and the common terms that fall under body, such as "ensouled," "living being" and "man," are called incorporeal (57). This is because none of these falls under sense-perception; each is grasped by the mind. For they have no defining properties through which they could be subject to perception. [?]

could be subject to perception. The individuals of which these are predicated, however, are bodies, since they fall under perception, for they have defining properties. The common body, and whatever falls under the common, is called incorporeal because it can be grasped only by the mind and in no way by the senses. Yet by nature it is still body. It is like the circle spoken of in general, which has no defining lines. Such a circle is measurable by nature, but because it has no defining lines it cannot be measured at all, for it has no defining cross-lines through which its size could be known. But when a circle becomes a particular one, defined specifically and definitely [?], its size can at once be measured and delimited. So the circle spoken of in general is by nature measurable in an indefinite way, but it cannot be measured definitely. In the same way, the human body assumed by the eternal Son is body [by nature]. But insofar as it is common, it does not fall under perception at all and is called incorporeal. Once it is marked out by defining properties, it at once falls definitely under perception and becomes perceptible and tangible.

Nor is the character formed by the properties some [other] thing, that is, a hypostasis. For in Christ the character belongs to nothing else, that is, to no other [hypostasis], than the eternal Son. In the same way, the character formed by the properties of each of us belongs to no one but the person whose character it is. Hence the eternal Son is one and the same, God and man. The same one who was begotten of the Father before all ages is Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary in the flesh [?] at the end of the ages, and he is one hypostasis of the Trinity. Therefore the all-pure and all-blameless maiden of David's line is properly and truly confessed as Theotokos. For she gave birth to the eternal Son himself, who became man like us in all things except sin and was called Jesus, just as one of us is called, say, Peter or Paul or some other proper name. It has been shown most clearly, then, that the eternal Son assumed a common thing, which is incorporeal, namely the human essence. Even so, it cannot be said that he did not become embodied, that is, become flesh and become man, as the deranged man heretically claims [?]. This too must be known: the heretics are eager to establish that nature is both common and particular. They say that the common nature is all the hypostases and the particular nature is one hypostasis. Their purpose is that this, once firmly established, may become a weapon for overthrowing the true and indestructible doctrine. For if what they agree on were true, someone could say to the most holy council assembled at Chalcedon: "Tell me, are these two natures that you proclaim in Christ common or particular?" If the council said they are common, he would at once reason against it: "Then by your account Christ is all the hypostases of the Godhead," which is absurd. But if it said they are particular, it would fall into the blasphemy of Nestorius by confessing two hypostases in Christ. Therefore the champions of the holy council and [?] must show that nature is called neither common nor particular in their sense. It is a common thing that escapes the absurdity of both alternatives. It is neither all the hypostases nor one hypostasis; it is what is contemplated and found whole [in each]. With God, the giver of light, this is demonstrated by proofs such as these. Every common thing is predicated. If, then, nature is said to be all the hypostases, all the hypostases will be predicated of each one of themselves. But what is predicated of many is [found] whole in each of the many of which it is predicated. It would then follow that all the hypostases are found in each one of themselves, which is impossible. So nature is not all the hypostases. For nature [?] ...

…understood by them as common, must be predicated of the hypostases, and not be called a nature, as they claim. This will be shown from what follows. For if the particular nature, as they understand it, is a hypostasis, then on their view the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit must necessarily be counted as three particular natures, and three gods and three godheads must be confessed. That is the most extreme of all blasphemies, or rather a complete denial of Christianity. So the deranged heretics have clearly shown that they speak senselessly when they say there is a particular nature. On every side the faith of the Orthodox is crowned against them with a royal diadem: the faith which confesses that Christ, that is, the eternal Son made man, is one hypostasis and two natures, the same at once God and man, the same being the subject of which the two natures are predicated. For each of the two natures is predicated of him, and gives him both its name and its definition. Hence the eternal Son is God, as the Father and the Holy Spirit are, and he receives the definition of God in the same way as each of them. The same eternal Son is also man, as each of us is, and he receives the definition of man, that is, a rational, mortal animal capable of knowledge, in the same way as each of us. Whoever says that Christ is one composite nature, just as he is one composite hypostasis, will likewise be forced to give a philosophical name both to this nature and to the hypostasis. He would certainly call the hypostasis the eternal Son incarnate. But what name will he be able to give to the nature? If he calls it God, he will deny the humanity. If he calls it man, he will abolish the Trinity. And if he calls it neither God nor man, he will then present Christ as neither God nor man. Besides the shame, he will fall into the greatest blasphemy and into the chasm of perdition. For what fitting name could the wretch find for this empty and sluggish nature, except "skindapsos" or "goat-stag" or some other such thing? But this above all you must know, most studious friends: when we Orthodox say that Christ is one composite hypostasis, we do not mean any hypostasis other than that of the eternal Son, who is one of the Trinity. We do not tolerate introducing some new one. God forbid! But let the manner of the hypostatic composition be explained. We say that the hypostasis of the eternal Son is composite in two ways. It is called composite from divinity and humanity, and it is also called composite in the way each human being is composed of soul and body. But the Lord is not said to be composite from divinity and humanity in the proper sense; he is said to be so metaphorically. For everything that is composite in the proper sense did not exist at all before the things from which it is composed were joined together. But we do not say that Christ simply did not exist at all before the coming together of the divinity and

humanity from which he was composed. Rather, we say that Christ was not "Christ" under that specific name before divinity and humanity came together in him. Since these came together hypostatically into an unconfused and unchangeable union, the term composition has been transferred to him from composition in the true sense, and he is called composite from divinity and humanity in a metaphorical way. For whatever is composed of things in the proper sense is called by a name different from the names of the things from which it was composed, since it has become a third result distinct from its components. When a human being is composed of soul and body, neither the soul nor the body is called by the name "human being." But Christ, composed in a certain way of the eternal Son and the humanity, is himself the eternal Son, even though he was not called Christ before his incarnation. That is why all the holy Scriptures, and the God-summoned council of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers at Nicaea, proclaim that the Lord Jesus Christ was begotten of the Father before all ages, that he made the ages, that he brought things from non-being into being, and that he is the Wisdom of the Father, and his Word and Power. But if what was composed of divinity and humanity, that is, Christ, were a new hypostasis besides the eternal one, then Christ would not be begotten of the Father before all ages. Nor would he be the maker of the ages, or the Wisdom, Word and Power of the Father. In this sense, then, the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the one composite hypostasis, is said to have been composed of divinity and humanity, but not in the way we say that every composite consists of its components. In a second way the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the incarnate, eternal, only-begotten Son of God, is said to be composed of soul and body, as we said earlier. For since the eternal Son, who is God by nature, became man [?] like us while remaining God, everything that is said of us is certainly said of him. Just as each of us is composed of soul and body, so he too, like us, is composed of soul and body. It has therefore been clearly shown that Christ is called composite in two ways, as we said before: from divinity and humanity, and from soul and body. He is the eternal Son, that is, the one hypostasis of the Trinity, who [?] with his Father, who has no beginning, and with his all-holy Spirit, to the endless ages of ages. Amen.

A. Every number that can be increased also has a limit. Now, we do not know how many human beings there are, but for the sake of brevity and clarity let us suppose that there are a hundred human beings in all. It is impossible that all of them were begotten. They do descend from one another, but when the mind traces the genealogy back upward, it must arrive at one who was not begotten. When we reach the first, we cannot say that he was begotten of another, since that one too would then have been begotten of someone else, until we come to rest at the first, unbegotten one. This first man, then, must either have grown out of the earth like plants, or be eternal, or have been made by some creator. If he had sprouted from the earth, the earth would still be sprouting others up to the present day, as it does with the kinds of trees and herbs. Since we do not see this happening, it is clear that the earth did not sprout the first one either. Nor was he eternal. If he had been eternal and without beginning, he would not have died or perished, for what has no beginning also has no end. It remains, then, that he was made, and what is made has a maker. So human beings have a Creator and Maker. Now take another proof that leads to the knowledge of God. Tell me: if I took a clod of earth, went up to a high room, and let it drop from there, would it not, being heavy by nature, keep falling downward until it came to rest on something more solid and immovable?

A. It is the same with the earth, for the whole is understood from the part. If the earth had nothing more solid beneath it to support it, it would never stop falling downward. Yet we see that it does not move. So there is some stronger power that supports and bears it, and this is the Word of God. If someone says that another body lies beneath it and supports it, what bears that body in turn? Reason keeps pressing the inquiry in this way and does not stop until it reaches some limit to the series of things being supported. For the earth cannot be unlimited below while being bounded above. What is bounded on one side clearly also has a limit on the other. Suppose a cord [?] ran from this side of the earth through to the other side, and I took hold of the visible end of the cord and pulled out two or three cubits. Would not the end on the other, unseen side necessarily be drawn upward by the same length that I pulled out? From this it can be clearly known that the earth has a limit below. These arguments have therefore proved that the things that exist have a maker.
B. You have proved it very well, and I am grateful to you for the benefit. But how will you prove that this maker [?]

A. Do you not know that what strikes is one thing and what is struck another, what sees is one thing and what is seen another, and what knows is one thing and what is known another? B. Yes, that is certainly so, for the same thing cannot be both agent and patient. A. And is God not simple, entirely unmixed, unblended and uncompounded? B. So one must say. A. Then how does what is simple in every way, and one in every respect, know itself? For it has been granted that the knower is one thing and the known another. This is seen most of all in things that are simple and have only one part. Among things made of parts, perhaps one part could see while another part is seen, and one could know while another is known. But such a thing necessarily brings in composition. God, however, admits no composition at all. He is beyond all immateriality and simplicity. So we must say one of two things. Either God knows himself, and so is composite, and [?] our first premise and agreement, that the knower is one thing and the known another, will be overturned. Or God remains ignorant of himself, which is itself completely absurd. B. The argument cannot be answered. A. Since both alternatives are absurd, how will God know himself while remaining in his simplicity? B. I cannot say how. A. All knowledge comes about in one of several ways. First, a thing is known from its own existence. When I see someone, for example, I know whether he is fair or dark, curly-haired or straight-haired, handsome or ugly, tall or short. Second, a thing is known from what is like it, that is, from what has the same essence and nature. How do you know, for example, that you have a heart, a liver, a spleen and the rest of the internal structure and arrangement, which you have never seen, except from another being of the same nature, from whom you learned that you yourself are made this way? Like things are understood from like things. Third, a thing is often recognized from some trace. If I pass through a field that has been ploughed and worked, I know from the trace that someone has worked it, even if I did not see the men who ploughed it. Again, if I see an arrow or a stone shot from some walled tower [?], I understand that someone has shot it. Fourth, someone is often known from an image. If I look into a mirror and see reflected in it the form of someone standing behind me and gazing into it, I know whether he is tall or short [?], snub-nosed, hook-nosed or large-eyed from the

likeness imprinted on the mirror. Fifth, opposites are often known from their opposites. When God said to Adam, "On the day you eat from the tree, you shall surely die," how did Adam know what death is, since he had never seen it? He had never seen anyone die. He could know it only from its opposite, that is, from life, for death is clearly the privation of life. In the same way the rich man knows poverty, and the healthy man knows sickness.

By which of these five ways, then, does God know himself? He cannot know himself from himself, for it has been granted that the knower is one thing and the known another. Nor can he know himself from some trace, for his works are far beneath him and inferior to him. Nor can he know himself through a mirror, nor by any of the four [?] ways. There must therefore be someone who is like him in every respect, that is, consubstantial and coeternal with God, from whom he may know himself, so that he is not left ignorant of himself. For when God sees his own Son, who is like him in every respect, he sees himself in him. The Son is the image of the invisible God and the imprint of his hypostasis. B. Let it be granted that God has someone coeternal and like him, so that he may know himself from him. How will you prove that this is a son? A. It befits lovers of justice to measure and weigh things back with the same measure and scale with which they themselves are measured and weighed. If I had received a hundred gold coins from you and wished to repay them, you ought to receive them back from me on the same scale on which I weighed them when I received them, and not on another. "A small weight and a large one my soul has hated," says God. How do we know that God exists, and what the properties of God are? Is it not from the things around us? If we have never seen him, and if we cannot understand him from his works either, we must remain in complete ignorance of God. So we describe God from the more honorable things around us, completely removing from what is said of God the accidents that attach to us. For example, among us there are life and death. Which should we use to characterize God, life or death? B. Clearly life. A. So we say that God is life and is living. But among us life has a beginning and an end, and it is needy. It requires a supply from outside: food, drink, breathing air and things of that kind, which sustain our life. So we set aside and remove all these accidents and defects, and we say that God lives a life, and a life of such a kind that it has neither beginning nor end, and needs nothing at all from outside. Or does it not seem so to you? B. You describe God quite wonderfully and very aptly from the things

around us, and there is no other way to know this or to say it. A. Consider the rest with me in the same way, my friend. Among us there is sight and blindness. Leaving blindness aside, we call God one who sees without being affected, that is, we banish the passive conditions of sight from him, for God is impassible in all things. Likewise there is hearing and deafness among us. We shall call God one who hears, not one who is deaf. The same goes for the rest. B. You have put it very well and acceptably. Now, most just of men, repay me the course of the argument on the same scale. A. Which is more precious among us, the fertile or the barren? Begetting or sterility? If you dispute this and are unfair about it, I too will dispute and claim that death is better than life, and that blindness and deafness are more honorable than sight and hearing. And what could be more absurd [?] or more ridiculous than that kind of dispute? B. You have truly proved that God is fertile and able to beget. All objection falls silent: begetting is more honorable than sterility and fruitlessness. But passions accompany begetting. A. But, my good and wise friend, we stipulated in advance that the Divine possesses the most honorable things that we have, without the passions and accidents that come with them. B. You have explained sufficiently, clearly and truly that God exists and that he has a Son. But why did God not beget more sons, so that he might rule and reign over more? A. Because one of three things would have had to happen. He would have begotten either infinitely many, forever and without end, or a fixed number, say a hundred, or one. If he had begotten countless sons and kept on begetting forever, his desire and good pleasure would never have been fulfilled. If he had begotten some fixed number, say a hundred, why would he have done so? Surely because one was not enough to fulfil all his good pleasure and desire, since that is why more would be needed. But if we granted this, the Son would be imperfect, needy and not self-sufficient. And if the Son is needy, and it has been shown that he is by nature equal and like to the Father, then God the Father too will be imperfect and needy (Lord, have mercy!) and not self-sufficient, which is absurd. But if the Son is perfect, and the Father is too, there is no need for others. Tell me, do you not say [?] A. And the other animals have no share in reason and free will?

B. That is so. A. If God wanted to send an apostle to us, that is, into the world, from what order would he send him? Surely from the angels or from human beings, for he would not send one of the irrational animals. B. That is so. A. Since these have free will, was it not up to the one being sent to obey God in the mission or not obey him, and either to say what he was commanded or to alter some of it [?]? You know that Moses, Jeremiah and others whom God sent at first begged to be excused and refused. Out of fear of the ministry, or under the sway of some other feeling, they made excuses, until God himself persuaded them with many words and exhortations. And if they had chosen to persist in this to the end, it was in their power to do so, since they had free will. B. That is so. A. Jonah even took flight from the face of the Lord to Tarshish when the Lord sent him to Nineveh. B. So we read. A. If, then, those who were sent either declined the mission or reported one message instead of another, one of two things would necessarily have happened. Either God's will would have come to nothing because he could find no apostle, or he himself would have had to rise from his royal throne and become his own apostle and messenger, the minister, agent and servant of his own will. But, as the argument has shown, it is entirely foreign and alien to royal dignity to carry out one's own wishes and commands personally. And to say that he would send us one of the irrational animals is foolish. It is absolutely necessary, then, that God have someone consubstantial with himself, who has free will and a will that does not differ from or conflict in any way with God's own will, to carry out his divine desires. This is the Son, who is coeternal with him, equal in perfection and one in counsel with him. In the Scriptures he is called the Angel of Great Counsel, and he spoke to the fathers of old, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses and the rest, as you will learn more precisely by reading the holy Scriptures. B. And what do you have to say about the Spirit? What need was there of him, since, as you have said, the Son is enough to make the Father's rule and kingdom complete? A. It is a mark of the most lawful kingship that the king never does anything himself, but accomplishes what he wills by command. If he does anything himself, that is a deficiency, a lowering and a degradation of kingship, and is not kingly. That is why the Son acts as mediator. Again, one of the most necessary things that make a kingdom complete is boundless and inexhaustible wealth, with treasuries and store-

rooms. For a king who is not generous, who does not enrich others or hand out gifts, is a poor and beggarly king. Or rather, he is no king at all. The royal wealth of the Father, then, is the Holy Spirit, who overflows with gifts. So the Father gives the Holy Spirit through the Son, that is, he gives the operations and graces of the Spirit. B. Then why does the Son not give himself, so that he himself becomes the wealth? A. Then the Son would be both the giver and the gift. That was untenable from the start, and we agreed on it when we said that the knower is one thing and the known another, and the agent one thing and what is acted upon another. So the Father commands as king, and the Son carries out the Father's good pleasure and gives the Holy Spirit, who is the wealth and the treasury of all good gifts. In this way the kingdom will be found complete, perfect and well ordered. B. But before creatures existed, there was no one to be enriched or to receive generosity. So there was no need for any Spirit. What need of him was there? A. My excellent friend, the kingdom of God must be perfect from eternity, so that it is not made perfect in time and only later, even if there were no one to share in it. In the same way, a philosopher or a physician wants to have his art and knowledge in perfect form even when there are no students or patients. You too are able to see even when you are asleep and lying down at night and are not actually seeing, because you are a complete human being. Whenever you want to see, sight is there for you; it does not come to you as something newly acquired at that moment. I will say to you about the Spirit what I said about the Son. The wealth of God is either greater than him, or equal to him, or less than him. It is not greater than him, for nothing is greater than God. Nor is it less than him, or we would [?] count it among the creatures, for whatever is less than God is a creature. Then God would at some point be poor, needy and lacking, which is unacceptable and absurd. It must therefore be equal and coeternal, so that God may be perfect and an eternal King. To him be glory and honor and might to the endless ages of ages. A letter containing the correct and blameless faith, sent by the blessed Pope [?] Thomas, patriarch of Jerusalem, to [?] in Armenia [?]. It was composed [?] by Theodore, surnamed Abu Qurrah, who was bishop of Harran, and translated by Michael, presbyter and synkellos [?] of the apostolic throne. It has been sent [?] to confirm [?] as the only true one the definition concerning faith in Christ our God that was set forth by the council convened at Chalcedon. Christ, our Lord and God, said to Peter, the leader of the apostles: "You are Peter, and [?]

"…on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it." The Lord spoke these words to Peter when Peter said to the Lord, who had called himself the Son of Man, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." So both statements came together in Christ our Lord, and it has been confirmed that he is God and man. Therefore, beloved, everyone who embraces Christianity must test and examine his own faith. If he finds that it affirms that Christ is both God and man, he ought to love it, hold fast to it and fight for it until the end of his life. But if in the end it turns out to be something else, he must loathe it, flee it and hate it, and must banish from his heart the harshness [?] and the attachment to the forebears from whom he inherited his faith [?], as David says: "Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty." For a person truly gains the beauty that is desirable in the eyes of Christ, the true bridegroom, the King of kings, only when he casts off his attachment to his fathers and shakes off his complacency [?] in holding on to what they handed down. Since this is how things stand, my friends, come, let all of us on both sides run together to the faith we have spoken of, the faith of this unshakable rock, the leader of the apostles, and let us believe that Christ is both God and man.

It must be understood that since Christ is both God and man, he is in every respect one hypostasis. Being both God and man, he has two natures, divine and human. Because he is properly God, he cannot fail to have a divine nature. And because he is truly man, he cannot fail to have a human nature by nature. This one hypostasis is the pre-eternal Son himself. Before all ages he was begotten of the Father timelessly and without passion. He is God, equal to the Father, and in his eternity he possesses the Father's essence as his own. In the last days this eternal Son became incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of Mary the Virgin, and he became man without change or alteration. He became like one of us in all things except sin. He took on our nature, which he did not have before, while the divine nature, which he had possessed from eternity, remained his. After his incarnation this eternal Son is himself both God and man. He is one hypostasis of the Trinity, having the nature of the Father and of the Holy Spirit and also our human nature, and yet the Trinity has received no addition. For indeed, my excellent friends, the very truth of what we have said makes it clear that the Trinity has taken on no increase. For we say that the one hypostasis which is God is the very one that is man [?], and not some other hypostasis.

But it is not true to say that because Christ is one hypostasis, he must therefore have only one nature. For it would inevitably follow that this one nature must be called either purely divine, or purely human, or divine and human together, or neither divine nor human. For if this one nature is purely divine [?] … then Christ is man and not God [?]. If this one nature is divine and human together, then it is the nature neither of the Holy Spirit [?] nor of men. Whoever holds this will be charged with blasphemy on both counts and will fall away from the nature he loves [?]. And if this one nature is neither divine nor human, then Christ is neither God nor man. So whichever way we turn the arguments, we are led to say that Christ is one hypostasis of the Trinity with two natures, a divine nature and a human nature. That is why both statements came together in him: his own, when he said of himself that he is the Son of Man, and Peter's, when he said of him that he is the Son of the living God. Whoever says that Christ is two hypostases makes Saint Peter answer Christ pointlessly, about something Christ had not asked. For if the one Christ asked about, the Son of Man, is a hypostasis other than the one who is the Son of God, then Peter's mind went astray, and his answer was about what he had not been asked, as we have said. If that were so (God forbid!), the Lord would not have praised his words, nor would he have called him blessed for the truth [?] and credited it to a revelation from the Father. [?] the truth of the confession about Christ, which the definition of the holy council of worthy Fathers assembled at Chalcedon rightly sets out when it defines Christ as one hypostasis of the Trinity with two natures, a divine nature and a human nature, as we have already said. And [?] an example: Let three gold coins be set out. [One?] was thrown [?] into the fire, and when it had been heated it became fire, while remaining the gold it was. Now if you put it in one place [?] with the other two gold coins, and in another place many burning coals, and then put the gold coin that was heated and became fire between the other two gold coins and the coals, the one in the middle [?] … the gold coin, having the complete nature of the other two gold coins [?], since it is gold, like each of those two coins, and also the nature of the [coals], since it is fire, like each of the other coals. But the middle gold coin [?] … one of the 'Trinity' of the gold coins, because it [has] the nature of the coals, which is fire, [yet] not [?] … from those coals a coal [?] …

…in the same way the eternal Son came down from heaven (let the hearers understand this descent in a way fitting for God). He took on not a hypostasis from us but our nature, and he became like one of us, apart from sin, as the divine Apostle himself says: "He was tempted in every way as we are, without…"

So the eternal Son has the nature of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, which he always had before, and also our human nature after his incarnation. He is one hypostasis of the Trinity and has received no addition, as was said before. But we must not make the nature a hypostasis, or the hypostasis a nature. Otherwise all of us Christians would have to say either that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three natures, just as they are three hypostases, or that they have one hypostasis, just as they have one nature. Both are foreign to the Christian confession, since the first is the view of Arius and the second that of Sabellius. The word of truth, as Gregory the Theologian said, is a Monad in Trinity and a Trinity in Monad, worshipped. The Monad is a monad of nature, not a monad of hypostasis, and the Trinity is a trinity of hypostases, not a trinity of natures. Whoever says that the nature is simply the collection of the hypostases will say that when Saint Gregory spoke of the Monad he was hinting at the Trinity. It will then be judged the same as if he had said "a Monad in a Monad" [?], and from there he will be driven to say "a unity in a unity". What could occur to anyone's mind that is more shameful? So one might rebuke whoever teaches this, saying: "I have the same authority over the words as you do. Just as you, having heard 'Monad' from the Theologian, take it to mean the Trinity itself, so I, hearing 'Trinity' from him, take it to mean a monad. Then the doctrine ends up for me as 'a monad in a monad'. And if you grant me this reading, as you granted yourself that one, the mind will be thoroughly confused [?], and the law of opposition and refutation will become useless." That cannot happen. But if you do not grant it, it will rightly be said to you that you are no examiner of words, since you rashly twist them to suit your own opinion without restraint. The words we have spoken about nature and hypostasis have now been recognized as true. So our view is fully confirmed: the natural Monad is distinct from the hypostatic Trinity, and the faith always abides in the confession of the natural Monad, as the divine Gregory said, together with the whole choir of holy and God-inspired Fathers. And if someone should say instead that nature is both common and particular, and that the common nature is all the hypostases while the particular nature is one hypostasis… [Variant readings:] 38 "worshipped" Turr.; 39 "you think" Turr.

…let him tell us when we ask: are the Father [and the Son] [?] … equal in nature, that is, consubstantial [?], or not? If he says that they are not [equal] in nature, he has completely cut himself off from Christianity. But if he agrees [?] … that the Father and the Son are equal in nature, let him answer us again: this nature, by which the Father and [the Son] are equal [?] … if he says that it is common, he will be forced to say that the Father and the Son are equal in three hypostases [?]. But if he says that the nature by which the Father and the Son are equal is particular, he will be compelled to say that the Father and the Son are equal in hypostasis, and it will follow for whoever says this that the Father and the Son are one hypostasis. Both consequences are very narrow [?] and [?]. The word of truth, then, which the confession of the holy Fathers gathered together at Chalcedon has established, is this: the nature is neither all the hypostases together nor one hypostasis. The nature always remains in the same unity, and the hypostases in the same Trinity, as the divine Gregory said when speaking of God. For he teaches us to know only this much: a Monad in Trinity and a Trinity in Monad, worshipped, which has a division and a union beyond all expectation. Nor may anyone say that if the natural Monad is distinct from the Trinity of hypostases, then the Monad [?] and the Trinity of hypostases make four things. For each of the hypostases is completed by the nature, and what completes a thing is not counted alongside the thing it completes. So the mind, at a loss in every [?] way, is carried by necessity to the most correct and blameless [?] confession of the council assembled at Chalcedon: that Christ is one hypostasis of the Trinity, having two natures, divine and human. And no one may say that if Christ is one hypostasis [?], he must inevitably also have one nature, or that if he has two natures, he must certainly also be two hypostases. The confession of the [?] council of the [?] Fathers assembled at Chalcedon has been ratified and made firm, since it does not depart from the faith of the leader of the apostles, which we set at the beginning. This confession is Peter's [?], against which the gates of Hades did not prevail. And [?] … it will be the end [?] of the whole Christian [?] at some time, even if Beliar, the enemy of [?] and of salvation, [?] many divisions against it, with Christ's permission. [?] … the divine [?] about it [?] … will never be abolished, and it will never be utterly defeated. It must also be said that since [the Son has] a divine nature [and] a human nature, he has two [?] energies and two natural [wills?] [?] … the assumption [?] is not confirmed if [?] … it should have whatever belongs to its own perfection. [?] … let the hearer understand our argument [?] … of the eternal [Son] are the two [?] … and energies of the [?] … one hypostasis [?] …

…of the Trinity, which, as we have clearly shown, has two natures together and belongs to no other hypostasis. For it is generally accepted, my friends, that one hypostasis can have different energies and still remain in its own unity. To give an example, we see that Paul is able to see, hear, speak and reason. Sight, hearing, speech and reasoning are different energies, each distinct from the others, but Paul is one hypostasis that has all four of these energies. Yet he sees with the eye and with no other member of the body. He hears with the ear and with no other, speaks with the tongue and with no other part, and reasons with the mind and with nothing else. Each of these hypostatic energies has a natural power in the nature [?], a matter underlying the act that the hypostasis performs, and what is performed belongs to the hypostasis. For example, Paul, being a hypostasis, has the power to speak by his own will, as all people do. But the words that Paul speaks at the moment he utters them are Paul's own. In the same way, then, we must not deny that the eternal Son, being one hypostasis of the Trinity, has after his incarnation both the divine nature, as the Father and the Holy Spirit do, and the human nature, as each individual human being does, in the way we have described. This being so, the divine nature is genuinely present in his hypostasis as the matter of the divine works he did during his incarnation and his life on earth. The human nature is likewise truly present in the hypostasis of the eternal Son as the matter of the human works he did while living among people, and these are his own, distinct from those of all other people. The same argument applies to his two natural properties and wills. It is also necessary not to leave the reader of this work in any doubt on this point: when we say that the eternal Son became man, we mean what Athanasius and Cyril, the hierarchs of Alexandria, and all the God-bearing Fathers have said. From the all-pure Virgin Mary he created for himself an ensouled [body] and a rational and holy soul, and he made them belong to his own hypostasis, just as a given person's flesh and soul belong to that person's hypostasis. A given person who has a human body and a human soul is a man. In the same way the eternal Son created a human body and a human soul for his own hypostasis, made both his own, and truly became man. And just as a given person's body and soul both belong to his own hypostasis

[?] and to no other human hypostasis, so for this reason we say that the eternal Son, being one hypostasis of the Trinity, has two natures. Neither of these belongs particularly to his hypostasis alone. The divine nature was his and also the Father's and the Holy Spirit's, and the human nature was his [?] and also that of individual human beings. His hypostasis, however, is set apart as distinctively his alone, distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit, and his body and his soul both belong particularly to his hypostasis, distinct from all other people. Whatever the flesh of the eternal one and his human soul underwent and suffered, the eternal Son himself is said to have undergone and suffered. It truly happened to him and is credited to him, just as whatever a given person's flesh and soul suffer happens to that person and is truly credited to him. That is why, confessing the true confession, we say that the eternal Son himself was hungry and thirsty, grew weary and was in agony; his face was struck and spat upon, and his back was scourged; the eternal Son's hands and feet were nailed; he himself hung on a cross, died and was buried, and rose on the third day. All these things, my friends, happened to the eternal one. But he suffered them in the way in which it was possible for him to suffer, that is, in his human flesh and soul, together with his divine nature [?]. If we wanted to explain in detail how each of these things happened, this work would be long and tiresome. But if we leave all of them unexplained, consider whether our words might then be closed to those who lack the sharpness needed to understand. So we single out death, the most hateful and hideous of the sufferings credited to the eternal Son. Once we have made this clear, we will show you how it happened to him and was credited to him, so that from what is said and heard [?] here you may be guided to the rest. My friends, as you know, John the Baptist was filled with the Holy Spirit while he was still in his mother's womb. John had a soul and a body. After the Holy Spirit came upon him, John's soul and John's body were [?] of the Holy Spirit. The death of any human being is the separation of his own soul from his own body. So when John's soul was separated from his own body, it was John who died, not the Holy Spirit who had come upon him. The death, therefore, was John's, and the Holy Spirit was free of it, so that John's death was not credited to the Spirit, in the way you have heard.

The eternal Son, however, was not joined to the hypostasis of some human being who had a body and soul. Instead he took human flesh and a human soul to himself, made both his own, and made them belong to his own hypostasis and to no other at all, just as John's body and John's soul belonged to no one else. In this way the eternal Son too became like one of us. When John's soul was separated from his own body, it was John himself who died, since the soul and body that were separated were his own. In the same way, when the human soul of the eternal Son was separated from his body, it was the eternal Son himself who died. For there was no other hypostasis there besides the eternal Son that had the body and soul which were separated, so that the death could be credited to that other hypostasis. But when John's soul was separated from his own body, he died and perished, for he existed only as the union of soul and body. The Son, however, who is before the ages, without beginning and eternal together with the Father, truly died when his human soul was separated from his own body, because the body and soul that were parted belonged to no other hypostasis, as we have already said. Yet he did not perish, since he always existed, even before he took this soul and flesh. In this way, then, the eternal Son truly died for us while remaining alive as he was. Our redemption came about not through the death of the hypostasis of some human being, such as John the Baptist, but through the death of the eternal Son, and he suffered no loss from it. This, my friends, is how the death of the eternal one came about. Anyone with sense can apply his own reflection [?] to all the human experiences in which he was involved [?] and understand how they came about. For whatever human experiences fall short of death are in some sense lesser [?]. If death may fittingly be spoken of the eternal Son in the way we have described, without suffering touching his divinity, then it is all the more fitting to speak of him in terms of the human experiences short of death, since no suffering touches his divinity. These human experiences, then, as was said before, happened to the eternal Son, who is Christ, after his incarnation: death, and everything else recorded in the holy Gospels. But we must by no means suppose that he endured any of these things under any compulsion at all. He endured them by his own free will. Yet whenever he chose to suffer these things, they happened to him in the natural way in which they happen to us. This was so that his saving dispensation would not be thought an illusion, and so that the sentence against the devil, from whom he redeemed the human race by this dispensation, would be just. To confirm what has been said, I will explain one kind of human experience that happened to him: let it be hunger. Whenever the eternal Son wished to be hungry, he allowed his flesh to take in the air…

[?] …power, so that the air at its surface is drawn in [?] through the pores of the skin. Then the part of the flesh nearest the air drew from the members it lay next to, from which the air is drawn up, and these in turn drew from the empty spaces. To these [?] a material supply from suitable food is provided, which was drawn from the veins that grow into them from the liver; the veins come from the liver, and the liver from the two veins that grow out of the stomach, and these two veins drew from the stomach. So the stomach, once emptied, sought a supply of food from outside. This, brothers, is how hunger came upon the eternal Son. He hungered by free will, not by natural necessity. A clear proof of this is that he went without food for forty days and only afterwards hungered. If the air had power over his flesh as it has over each of ours, he would not have gone one day, or two, or three, before becoming hungry, as we see happen in our case [?]. But when he chose, he allowed nature the occasion to do and show what belongs to it. In the same way he also endured death willingly. Hear the Truth itself saying this about it: "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again. And no one takes it from me." So that you may understand what is said more clearly, I will add this. God fashioned Adam's body pure of all defilement. No natural, blameless passion ruled over it by necessity: not death, nor the passions that come before death, nor those that come after it. But when Adam, by his own free choice and will, transgressed the divine commandment, fell under sin and was defiled, he was enslaved to and mastered by the natural, blameless passions: death, and those that come before death and after it. That is why Adam was forced by necessity to hunger, to thirst and to die, and after death [?] the corruption of his body held sway over him, and so with everything like these. The eternal Son, however, took up the Adamic body. That is, he formed it for himself from the spotless blood of the all-holy Virgin Mary, pure and free of every stain of sin. For this reason death had no power over it, nor did the swarm of passions that come before death, by which I mean hunger and the other natural, blameless passions, as we have shown. Nor did the corruption of bodies after death have power over it. David, the ancestor of God, foretold this in song: "You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption." Why [?] should I go on listing particulars instead of speaking in summary? The body of the eternal Son, from the beginning of its formation and of its unconfused hypostatic union with the eternal Son, was deified with the most perfect deification. Without change, it became that which anointed it, and I dare to say, one in Godhead with it. But the eternal Son, being willing,

allowed it to live in the manner of human bodies. He did this so that he might escape the devil's notice and his saving dispensation might be made credible, so that the body might experience sorrows and undergo the passions, and so that he might endure death for us in truth and not in appearance. Having fulfilled his whole dispensation, after his resurrection from the dead he displayed in his own flesh the glory of his Godhead. Someone might think that this glory, displayed in the flesh of the eternal Son after he rose from the tomb, came in from outside, and not that it was the manifestation of what had been hidden in that flesh from the beginning through the unconfused hypostatic union. There is clear testimony against this. Before his saving passion, in the presence of three of his disciples on Mount Tabor, he showed the divine glory in his flesh, the same glory he also revealed after his return from the dead. For, as we said before, the flesh of the eternal one had been deified with the most perfect deification from the beginning of its formation. But for the reason we mentioned, the eternal Son let it conduct itself according to the way our bodies live. This, then, sirs, is the outline of our confession. We could go through it at greater length, but I have declined to make my discourse long. So understand what we have set out for you, and accept it in the love of Christ. Join with us and be united, and let us all become one through the eternal Spirit in this God-inspired confession of Peter, the great chief of the apostles, which we have set out [?]. Then Christ our God may be gracious to us, drive away every hostile assault and every grievous affliction, bring us into true blessedness, and join and fit us into his kingdom. May all of us attain it, through the intercessions of our all-holy Lady, Mary the Theotokos, of John the Forerunner and Baptist, of Peter the chief of the apostles, of James the brother of God, and of the whole company of the saints. By the same Theodore Abu Qurrah, bishop. [?] Question. Why do we say that the humanity of Christ is the humanity of Peter and of Paul and of individual men, but do not say that the body of Christ, which we receive, is the body of Peter and of Paul and of each individual man? Answer. When what is common receives a material, characteristic property, it becomes a hypostasis. But when body, spoken of as common and in general terms, receives a characteristic property, it is no longer called "so-and-so" but "so-and-so's." That is, it does not become a hypostasis but belongs to the hypostasis. For the body is a part of the [?]

nature, and not the whole. So the part does not subsist on its own [?], but is spoken of as belonging to the whole. An example showing how the defilement of Adam's sin passed to the whole human race. Farmers say that if you take a vine branch, dip it in oil and plant it, the whole quality of the oil is passed into the fruit too, that is, into the grape. In the same way Adam received nature pure, stained it with sin and the passions, and the quality was passed on to us. How the cleansing passed to all of us through the Saviour's incarnate dispensation. They also say that if you take a melon seed, dip it in honey and sow it, the sweetness of the honey is passed into the fruit as well. In the same way Christ cleansed nature of the oily quality, that is, of sin, through holy baptism, and took it up spotless and undefiled, as it had been when it was first created. He dipped it in the honey of the Godhead, in sweetness, that is, in the power of the Paraclete, and gave us a share in the sweetness, as melon seeds pass it to the fruit that comes from them, and on down the line.

By the same Theodore, bishop of Harran, on Christ's wrestling with the devil. Question. If Christ, who is God, wrestled with the devil and won, what great thing has he done? The devil will say, "I defeated a man and was defeated by God." And what did our nature gain when God won? Answer. The Jacobites say simply that God the Word wrestled and won. The Nestorians, on the other hand, say simply that the man alone did. But the Church, travelling the middle and royal road, teaches that God the Word carried on the struggle with the devil in the flesh. If, as the Nestorians say, it was a man who won and was put to death, a man's death did us no good. I leave aside for now that they will stumble many times before they prove that a mere man could have won. And if it is as the Jacobites say, a victory won by God alone is nothing to us. But since [?] Adam and the people after him, the devil, seeing them defeated by him, did not count the defeat against the hypostasis of Adam and of the other people, but against the nature itself. He said, "God fashioned a creature that cannot stand against me and against sin." For this reason God the Word took up the complete nature of humanity and used its

free will, its senses and all its natural powers according to nature, as was fitting and in accordance with God's will. That is how he defeated the devil. He did not add and supply divine power beyond nature in the struggle. Instead he used what is natural in a fitting way, in harmony with God's law, and ordered all the parts, powers and organs of the nature properly, within the measures of humanity. So he won, and showed the nature to be victorious, and from then on the victory and the justification are counted to the nature. B. Tell me, was the human mind the one wrestling with the devil? Or, to put it simply, was it self-moved or moved by another? A. Your mind, or foot, or hand is not said to move itself, for it is you who move and direct your mind, your members and your powers as you wish. In the same way God the Word was the one who moved and governed his own human mind, senses, natural habits and powers as he wished. As for what you said, whether Christ's mind was self-moved or moved by another, this is our answer. The nature, that is, the soul and the body with its parts and sense organs, each has a simple, natural motion of its own. If they did not have some natural motion, we could not move them. So we take up this natural, simple motion and move and direct it as we wish, well or badly. For example, the feet naturally have the motion of walking, but I use walking as I wish. The eyes have simple seeing, but I use sight as I wish. So I have seeing from nature, but how I see comes from myself. The same holds for willing and the other parts of nature, and for the mind itself. The mind too naturally has simple reasoning, about this or that. But I use this natural power of the mind as I choose, thinking good things or bad and putting the mind's power to work toward whatever I desire. Simple motion, then, belongs to the property of each part of the nature, while how it moves belongs to the hypostasis. Understand it in the same way in Christ's case. A carpenter is said to have made the chair with his own hand, and we also say that the carpenter's hand made the chair. In the same way we say that God the Word won by means of the flesh, and we also say that the flesh, that is, the nature of humanity, won. B. How was Adam defeated? Was it not by doubting, or rather by disbelieving God's word and believing the

[?] …are not free of blame, but also owe thanks [?]. Tell me, as I put a question to you in turn: I blaspheme [?] every day, as you say, [?]. Do I do this against his will or with his will? If against his will, he is weak. If with his will, then [?] taxes and tributes ought not to be demanded of me; instead I should receive gifts, since I am fulfilling the will of your god. Answer me something else. When you go campaigning in Roman lands and one of you is killed there, does he not certainly go to paradise, as you teach? B. Yes, certainly. A. Suppose you had gone with your own brother and campaigned against the Romans, and [someone] killed your son. Would you punish the one who killed him as an enemy and kill him in return, or would you honour him as a benefactor and embrace and kiss him? B. Of course I would kill him ten thousand times over and cut him limb from limb, if I could. A. Then how can you judge it right to kill the one who brought your brother such salvation and delight? Tell me about another case too. Suppose you had a very painful and deadly sore on your eye. One of your enemies wanted to deal you a fatal blow and rid you of life quickly. Seizing his chance, he struck you nowhere else on your body but on the wounded eye, so as to rid you of life as quickly as possible, as I said. As it happened, the struck eye discharged pus, fluid and moist rot, and you were freed from the pain by that blow and became completely healthy. Would you then regard the enemy who struck you as a friend and benefactor? Would you ignore his intention and love him and do him good because of what happened against his intention and against his will? B. No, I would punish him limb by limb if I had the power, as the most hateful and hostile

A. Think in the same way about the benefits the Jews conferred on us against their will. The same man held a debate with a Jew. A: the Christian. B: the Jew. B. I, he says, will argue with you from the Scriptures, for I know nothing else besides them. [Notes:] 37 "son and". 38 "brother". 39 "son".

A. Nor do I reject them. But I must first make clear to the hearers present how I understand the Scriptures. Suppose someone enters a house where, say, Paul is painted, and sees the image. He points to it and says, "This is Paul of Tarsus, who stood by approving the killing of Stephen, who received letters from the high priests and set out for Damascus, ravaging the Christians and putting them in prison. This is the man who was turned to Christianity by divine power through a vision and became the herald and teacher of the nations," and he says other things of the kind. The one gazing at Paul's image refers all these things to the Paul who is depicted, whose image it is, and not to the painting or the colours. But suppose he says, "The painter did not portray Paul well. He made his shoulders far too broad, he did not get his eye right, he made his legs thin or stunted," and so on. These things are not referred to the person portrayed but are confined to the image alone. So too in Scripture, among the things said about the saints, some refer to Christ, who was imaged and prefigured through them, while others [?] apply to them alone. Does this way of reading and explaining Scripture satisfy you, Jew? B. No. I do not accept it. Rather, [?] according to the letter: what is said of David, for example, I understand of him alone, and likewise what is said of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah and the rest. A. Look at what you are saying, and know that [?]

A. So the Word of God [?]. B. He is going to give them the land, he says. A. But God did not speak like that, saying, "I am going to [?] it to your children." He said, "To you and to your seed." Likewise he said to Jacob, "This land, which I gave to your fathers, Abraham and Isaac, I will give to you, and to your seed after you." Yet Jacob did not have even a foot's length of ground either, and he died in a foreign land, in Egypt. Do you see that whoever understands the Scriptures this way makes God a liar? And what of his saying to Jacob, "Nations and a gathering of nations shall come from you"? [?] how were the nations born of Jacob? Again he said to him, "The sons of your

father shall bow down to you. And he and your seed shall rule over them." How could he say "your brothers" in the plural, when Jacob had only one brother, Esau? And where did Esau ever bow down to Jacob? On the contrary, it was Jacob who bowed to the ground seven times before Esau and called him lord, and he went on fearing and trembling before him his whole life. Moreover, many years later, when they had come out of Egypt, Moses sent word to the first man and ruler of the sons of Esau: "We are your brothers. Allow us only to pass through your land. We will go by the king's highway; we will not turn aside to the right or to the left. We will even pay for water and bread, until we have passed through to the land that God has given us." And he sent word back to them: "No. If you pass through my land, we will come out and kill you." God did not overturn this. Rather, he confirmed and upheld it, saying, "This land, which I have given to Esau: do not go near them," and so on. Where, then, did God fulfil for Jacob what he said: "The sons of your father shall bow down to you, and your brothers, and you and your seed shall rule over them," and the like? Do you see, Jew, that everywhere you make God a liar through your bad interpretation and your lack of understanding? Did not God appear to Jacob when he wrestled with him and say to him, "From now on your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel"? Yet countless times afterwards God, and Scripture, and Jacob himself called him Jacob. Why, then, have God's words not failed, and are they not unreliable on this reading? B. Another question, showing by an illustration that Muhammad is an enemy of God and was troubled by a demon.

Suppose a king who ruled all the creation under heaven learned that the inhabitants of some country were reviling him and insulting his power. In his anger he sent a general to them to stop their reviling and teach them to speak well of him, or, if they would not comply, to punish them with the sword. But when the general reached the country of these insolent people, he took a bribe. Instead of stopping them, he urged them to insult the king even more, and in return for the money he wrote them an exhortation to do so in his own hand. Is anyone more hostile to the king than the man who dared to do this? I think no one. But perhaps someone will say: "Would anyone go so far in madness as to urge people to revile his own master, taking gold for the reviling?" I would answer him: the madman did, Muhammad, the false prophet of the Hagarenes, as we find him boasting in his own lies. For he said, in a demonic frenzy: "God sent me to shed the blood of those who say that the Divine is a nature in three hypostases, and of all who do not say: 'God is one, God is solid, who has not begotten and was not begotten, and no one has been his partner.'" This is the theology of a madman. He denied that God is the begetter of light and the one who sends forth sanctification. He boasted that God had commanded him to punish the Christians with the sword as revilers who insulted the Godhead. Yet he was won over by money, and so, possessed by a demon, he allowed them to insult the one who had sent him, as he supposed.

And so that no one thinks we are lying when we call him possessed by a demon, let him read the story they have entitled "The Pardon of Aisha." She was his wife. He suspected her of adultery and drove her away to her parents. Some days later, as he was sitting with them,

he fell into a demonic fit and writhed about, so that those present said a very heavy oracle had come down upon him. After a little while he came to his senses and was asked what had happened. He said: "The pardon of Aisha has come down upon me." And as though an angel had assured him that she was clear of suspicion, he took her back.

When you hear this, you gnash your teeth and rush to kill him, but you cannot. So you take up the question again and answer: 'Tell us plainly this preaching of yours that is so hard to accept.' He says: 'The Son of God came down from heaven and took flesh from a woman. He became man and was brought up as an infant. Hunted by his enemies, he fled as a refugee into Egypt. and they array themselves against him from every side, striving to show that he is neither God nor the Son of God.
