The Saracen: And is it possible for God to have [a Son?]

Theodore: It is not possible for God not to have a Son.
The Saracen: How, and in what way?
Theodore: Is it possible for God not to rule?
The Saracen: Certainly not.
Theodore: And over whom does God rule?
The Saracen: Over his own creatures.
Theodore: Then ruling has come to him as an accident and not by nature, and he could be said to have his rule as something brought in from outside and acquired, recent and not co-unoriginate with him. For before the creatures, as you say, he did not rule. Instead the creatures became the cause of his rule, having elected him over themselves as ruler, when before he was not one by nature. He would then owe them thanks, as having been granted the honor of rule through them. And if he decided that they should return to non-being, he would be left without subjects, and from then on, by your account, he would be stripped of rule over the ruled. And besides so many absurdities, another would necessarily follow [?].

Theodore: Those who are ruled are of three kinds: either greater than the ruler, or lesser, or equal. To rule over greater ones [?] is blasphemous, for nothing is greater than God. To rule over lesser ones is dishonorable, given the absurdities already mentioned. It remains to say that he rules over equals who are co-unoriginate with him.

The Saracen: And who is equal to God and co-unoriginate with him, and yet ruled by him?
Theodore: Those who are ruled are of three kinds. One is ruled because he wills it; another because he is under tyranny; another neither by willing nor by tyranny. But God does not rule those who have chosen it, lest they choose again and replace him; and in that case his rule would not be co-unoriginate, nor would he have it by nature, for it would come after their choice, and so be recent and dishonorable, as has been said. Nor does he rule those under tyranny, for that is unbecoming, along with the other absurdities. It remains then to say that God rules one who is ruled neither by willing nor by tyranny, but by natural rule.
The Saracen: And who is the one ruled by God naturally

Theodore: Rulers are of three kinds. One rules by the vote of the ruled; another by tyranny; another by nature. God does not rule by the vote of the ruled, because of the accidents mentioned before, which it is unfitting to say of God. Nor does he rule by tyranny, for tyranny is driven far away from God. So the third mode remains, according to which God is said to be ruler, above every vote and free of all tyranny, which is

The Saracen: And who is the one ruled by God naturally?
Theodore: His Son, through whom God is known as Ruler and Father without beginning; for everything natural comes before deliberate willing.
The Saracen: What do you mean, for example?
Theodore: Before we want to breathe, we breathe; before we want to hear, we hear; and before we want to see, we see. See then, you who deny the divinity of the Word of God: it has been demonstrated that God has a Son, consubstantial, co-unoriginate and co-eternal, who shares the throne of the Begetter in the supreme dignities of the Godhead; who as Creator and Master is served and worshiped together with him by all creation, invisible and visible; who has heaven for his throne and the earth for his footstool; and further, to speak prophetically, who measures heaven with a span and the earth with a handful, before whom all the nations are as the tip of a balance and as a drop from a bucket.
A dialogue by the same, demonstrating that the Father always begets and the Son is always begotten.
Heretic: What do you think? Has everything that has come to an end had a beginning, or not?

Orthodox: Certainly.
Heretic: Then if the one begot and the other was begotten, and these things have passed—that is, the Father's begetting and the Son's being begotten—and things that have passed have come to an end, and such a thing had a beginning, as is agreed, then the Father's begetting had a beginning, and so did the Son's being begotten. So the Father's being Father had a beginning, and likewise the Son's being Son. Or do you not think this has been correctly reasoned?
Orthodox: Not at all.
Heretic: Why not?
Orthodox: If “he begot” and “he was begotten” were said of God in a temporal sense, there would be a difficulty [?]. But since the pious mind takes these things eternally, they are no longer to be understood as past but as always being. Just as God “was,” not as having an existence that is past—for he always is—so too with “he begot” and “he was begotten.”
Heretic: Then the generation is incomplete, if the one always begets and the other is always begotten. Or is that not so?
Orthodox: Certainly not. For the Father always is, and likewise the Son; so by your reasoning the existence of both the Father and the Son is incomplete, because it does not come to an end. Rather, the most complete thing is this: what has its end from itself and is always in its end, and does not have it added from outside. Further, the Son's being begotten signifies nothing other than his having existence from the Father; and he always has existence from the Father; therefore he is always begotten. For the Son in the proper sense had to have his existence from the Father always, and not as we do, who have only the beginning of it. “Being begotten” is used equivocally. In our case it is a way into existence; but in the case of the Son of God it signifies existence itself, not a way into existence. They differ only in mode: being, taken by itself, is existence, but understood as being from the Father, it is called being begotten. Since, then, two meanings of “being begotten” have been shown, in the first sense it is absurd to be always begotten, but in the second not at all. For in the first sense of being begotten the end is existence, and if it does not reach its end it is incomplete. But with the Son of God it is not

so. For the Son of God's being begotten does not have existence as its end; it is itself the end, and it is complete. Since, then, it has been shown that the Son is always begotten, that is, always has his being from the Father, the Father therefore always begets, that is, is always the cause of the Son. Let these points be settled in this way.
A scholion by the same.
So the problem that seemed difficult has been solved—I mean the question whether he begot him when he was or when he was not. For this signifies nothing other than whether he was the cause of his being when he was, or when he was not. Whatever answer it is fitting to give to this question, the equivalent answer will be fitting for the equivalent question before us. Since, then, the Father is always the cause of the Son's being, it is clear that the Son always being, the Father is his cause. [So] when he was, the Father was his cause. And this is the same as saying “he begot him when he was”; therefore he begot him when he was. And this is not absurd. For in the case of God “he begot” does not mean bringing something forth from himself out of non-being into being; if it did, “he begot him when he was” would be absurd. But as we have defined it, it is not at all [absurd?].
By Theodore Abu Qurrah, the philosopher, bishop of Harran, on the names of God.
The name “God” is derived from a certain activity, yet it does not signify the activity but the nature that acts. For if the name “God” indicated an activity, and every name is the name of what it indicates, then the name “God” would be the name of an activity. So what is named “God” would be God's activity. Then God's activity would be God, and God would be his activity. So God and God's activity would be the same, which is impossible. If someone should contentiously say that it is not impossible to posit this, let him know that many absurdities follow which he would have to admit. First, being said in relation to the same thing. For things that are the same are said in relation to the same thing, if indeed they admit the same [definition]. But activity is said to be “of God,” while God is not said to be “God of God.” Further, activity is the activity of an agent, but God is not the God of an agent. Further, if God and God's activity were the same, both would be predicated of the same things. But “God” is predicated of the Father, the Son and the Spirit, whereas “activity” is not predicated in the same way. For the Father is God, and likewise the Son and the

Spirit. But the Father is not an activity, nor is the Son, nor the Spirit; rather, they are active. And the greatest absurdity is to say that God does not exist before his activity but simultaneously with it, for things that are the same must be acknowledged to be simultaneous. If, then, God is eternal, his activity is eternal too. So the effect of the activity is eternal as well. And the effect is the world; therefore on the proposed hypothesis the world is eternal—which is not only impossible but also impious to say. Further, everything that is predicated most properly and most fully of all the hypostases under it is either a nature or a part of a nature. God is predicated most properly and most fully of three hypostases; therefore God is either a nature or a part of a nature. But since part is impossible in God, it remains that it is

[nature, and that the name] indicates nature [?]. For just as the name [“man”?] is derived from some activity, yet signifies not [the activity] but the nature and the essence, so too “soul” and “angel,” and nearly all names of essences, are derived from an activity or a passion, yet signify not an activity or passion but essence and [nature?]. Understand it in the same way, I ask you, in the case of God, lest you go astray by following etymologies and grammatical rules and overlooking the rule of truth, which many profess to use, but few actually do. As for the end, we pray for it, with God's help.
Dialogue of a heretic with an Orthodox on God and Godhead.
Heretic: What do you think? Are God and Godhead the same, or different?
Orthodox: The same.
Heretic: Are not the same things predicated of the same thing?
Orthodox: Not necessarily.
Heretic: If these are the same, [how are they not] predicated of the same thing? And if they are not predicated of it, how are the same things not different? Which is impossible.
Orthodox: For the same things to be predicated of the same thing it is not enough that they be the same; it must also be the case that they are understood and spoken of in the same way. Now God and Godhead are for us the same, but the mode differs; that is, God and Godhead are not understood in the same way. When we think and say “God,” we think and say the nature in a hypostasis; but by “Godhead” we mean the nature itself, as alone and considered without hypostasis. For this

reason we predicate “God” of the hypostasis, since God is considered in a hypostasis; but we do not predicate “Godhead” of it at all, since Godhead is taken by itself and considered without hypostasis. For it must be understood that the Godhead does not exist without the three hypostases, but when considered by itself it is considered without the hypostases. Considering a thing in this way does not rule out its existence. Since the Godhead, when conceived by itself, is nature without properties [?], it is clear that it is also without hypostases. For if it were conceived by itself together with hypostases, it would plainly be conceived with properties too, which was not the supposition. Further, what cannot be conceived without something else must be a relative, and not an essence. But the Godhead is not a relative; it is a superessential essence; so it can be considered by itself alone and not together with something else. Further, a man does not exist without a place, yet when he is considered and defined by himself, he is considered and defined without a place. Again, the soul of a man, while he lives, does not exist without a body, yet when it is considered by itself it is considered without it. So too the Godhead does not exist without the hypostases, but when it is considered by itself, it is considered without them.

Heretic: Are essence and hypostasis different things?
Orthodox: They are different, not as one thing and another thing, but in that the hypostasis signifies one thing and the essence another. A grain of wheat is called both seed and fruit, not as one thing and another thing; yet “seed” signifies one thing and “fruit” another: the seed is seed for the coming harvest, the fruit is fruit of the past one.

Heretic: What does essence signify, and what does hypostasis?
Orthodox: Essence signifies what is common, and whatever is proper to the essence is common to the hypostases under that essence. The hypostasis has a property that is not common to the hypostases of the same essence, and it also admits of number.
Heretic: Does essence, then, have no property?
Orthodox: It does not share in a property, since such a property is not common to the hypostases of the essence; nor does one essence admit of plural number. For what admits of plural number certainly has a property, and what has a property admits of number, for it is the property itself that introduces number.
Heretic: I don't understand what you are saying. Say it more clearly [?].
Orthodox: Do you call the essence of the Father [?]

[?], and invisible, and incorruptible, and [?], and God?
Heretic: Yes.
Orthodox: And the Son likewise?

Orthodox: And do you call the Son Father?
Heretic: No.
Orthodox: Then “Father” is not proper to the essence but to the hypostasis.
Orthodox: For the properties of the essence are common alike to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, but “Father” is not common. And if the property of the essence is one thing and that of the hypostasis another, they do not signify the same thing.
Heretic: Is not unbegottenness proper to the Father, begottenness to the Son, and procession to the Spirit? Why then do you not also say three essences?
Orthodox: Because properties must be assigned to number [?]; and property is otherness. Otherness [of essence] makes things of different essence; and what is of a different essence is not equally eternal, not equally incorruptible, and so on. [?] the essence of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is one. When we say three hypostases, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, [we mean] in truth [?] the difference of the properties in the hypostasis, and not [?]
Heretic: If there is one Godhead, there is also one hypostasis.
Orthodox: Godhead signifies the being that is the same [?] in the hypostases, whereas hypostasis signifies being something particular; but [?] identity [?]. For not every hypostasis is Godhead, just as not every hypostasis is humanity. And if not every hypostasis is Godhead, then hypostasis does not signify the same thing [as Godhead].
Heretic: Does humanity not subsist? [?]
Heretic: Then it is a hypostasis.
Orthodox: [It subsists] as considered in individuals.
Heretic: What is an individual, and what is humanity?
Orthodox: An individual is the hypostasis of each one of us; humanity is what is common in the essence.
Heretic: And what is the difference between what is common and [?]
Orthodox: Because your hypostasis does not belong to all human beings, whereas humanity is common to all.

Heretic: Is the hypostasis of the Father not Godhead?
Orthodox: Yes. But Godhead signifies being, while hypostasis signifies being a particular someone.
Heretic: And is the hypostasis of the Son not Godhead?

Heretic: Then there are two Godheads.
Orthodox: No. There is not one Godhead and then another.

Heretic: There is one hypostasis and then another.
Orthodox: But I did not say that Godhead and hypostasis signify the same thing. Godhead signifies being, while hypostasis signifies being a particular someone. Just as Paul and Peter are not two humanities, so the Father and the Son are not two Godheads.
Heretic: Then is the hypostasis of the Father not [?] and

Orthodox: The hypostasis of the Father is Godhead, and the hypostasis of the Son is Godhead. But it does not follow that because there are two hypostases there are also two Godheads.
Heretic: Why not?
Orthodox: Because the hypostasis of the Father is immortality, and the hypostasis of the Son is immortality too, yet there are not two immortalities.
Heretic: How so?
Orthodox: Because there is no difference within immortality. Immortality differs in no way from immortality, if it is immortality.
Heretic: If there really is one hypostasis and then another, how is there not also one immortality and then another?
Orthodox: We too each have our own hypostasis, but we do not each have our own humanity. Peter's hypostasis is humanity, and Paul's hypostasis is humanity, yet they are not different humanities. We each have our own hypostasis, but we do not each have our own immortality, the immortality we received through the one baptism. If there were one immortality and then another, there would be one baptism and then another, and one faith and then another, and it would no longer be "one Lord, one faith, one baptism."
Heretic: But if our faith is something other than immortality and baptism, then the hypostasis of God is something other than immortality.
Orthodox: Not at all. That very hypostasis is also immortality, and not only immortality but also incorruption and righteousness. God is not composite. He is called by these names according to distinctions in our way of conceiving him. He is called immortality because he has no end, incorruption because he is [?], righteousness because of his fairness, sanctification because he guards from sin,

redemption because he saves our life from corruption, lordship because he rules over all things, and power because nothing can oppose him. All these are also seen in the hypostasis of the Son, as they are in the Father, and not by participation. That is why we speak of two hypostases, of the Father and of the Son, but of one Godhead, [?] one authority and one power.
Heretic: Is not everything that is predicated of something predicated either essentially or accidentally?
Heretic: And does not everything that belongs essentially to something [?] also belong to all things consubstantial with it?

Heretic: And are not the things predicated accidentally separable, whether in thought or in fact?
Orthodox: Yes.
Heretic: Then how does the name "Father" belong to the Father? If it belongs essentially, it will also belong to [?]. But if it belongs accidentally, then the Father can at some point be conceived of as not being Father. And again, if accidental things come after essences, then by nature [?] "Father" will still [?]. And [?] the Son Father, and likewise [?]

IX. Dialogue of the same author with a Nestorian.
Orthodox: Look, the contest of debate is before us. Where should we begin our discussion? With the [?] arts, or rather first with the most necessary of the other questions? And which of the [?] disputed points of the faith should come first [?]?
Heretic: By all means we should begin with matters of the faith.

Heretic: Nature.
Orthodox: Then did he assume it with its properties, or without them?
Heretic: He assumed the nature alone, without the properties.
Orthodox: In that case it was without color, without shape, without a blending of the elements, and without size. So it could not be recognized, or seen, or held, and it did not grow from a child into a man. What, then? Do you profess that in Christ color, shape, and the other things I listed were done away with?
Heretic: God forbid!
Orthodox: Then you profess that they existed?
Heretic: I do.
Orthodox: Well then, are these not properties?
Heretic: Of course they are.
Orthodox: So Christ had our nature with its properties. And a nature with properties is a hypostasis. Or do you not think so?
Heretic: Certainly I do.
Orthodox: Then he assumed a hypostasis, and not the nature alone, as you proposed.
Heretic: So it is.
Orthodox: But that too is impossible.
Heretic: And how can you show this?
Orthodox: Either the hypostases were united, or they remained separate. If they remained separate, Christ will be two and not one. If you worship Christ as two, and also worship the Father and his Spirit, you are in danger of worshiping a quaternity. But if the hypostases were united into one composite hypostasis, that composite hypostasis will be neither purely divine nor purely human, but something between the two. And if Christ is a composite hypostasis, then on your account Christ is neither a divine hypostasis nor a human one, but something between God and man. We must shun such impiety. So how do you resolve the argument for us?
Heretic: I am quite unable to. Do me the favor, then, and teach me: what did Christ assume, a nature or

Orthodox: A nature.
Heretic: With its properties, or without them?
Orthodox: With its properties.
Heretic: Then he assumed a hypostasis?
Orthodox: Certainly not.
Heretic: And how is that clear?
Orthodox: I will explain it to you. There is something called a hypostasis, and there is something called hypostatic, that is, belonging to a hypostasis. Both have this in common, that they are composed of a nature and properties. They differ in that a hypostasis is not part of anything, so that [Peter] is a hypostasis. But the body of Peter is a part,

since it belongs to Peter. So the body of Peter is hypostatic and not a hypostasis, even though it is a nature with properties. For a hypostasis to come into being, it is not enough for a nature to be composed with properties. Something else must also be true of it: it must not be a part. Since the ensouled body that was assumed is part of Christ, it is not a hypostasis but hypostatic. Peter's body is not counted alongside Peter so as to make two, for the one is joined together with the other. In the same way, the ensouled body that was assumed is not counted alongside the incarnate Son of God so as to make two. I think this has been said clearly enough to resolve the difficulty.

Another dialogue of the same author with a Jacobite.
Heretic: Do you think Christ is God or man?
Orthodox: Both, and each of the two.
Heretic: How?
Orthodox: He is God by himself, and likewise man, and at the same time God and man.
Heretic: Then is he these things by nature, or [?] by grace, or by some discipline and progress?
Orthodox: By nature.
Heretic: Then God and man are of one nature?
Orthodox: You are mistaken. He is not man and God by the same nature. He is man by one nature and God by another.
Heretic: Then, since God and man are different by nature, and Christ is both, is Christ different from himself?
Orthodox: Not at all. He is different in nature. That is the conclusion you should draw from what has been agreed. But what are you saying? [?] You have said [?]: Christ is God and man; God and man are different in nature; therefore Christ is different in nature. So you have tricked yourself. Being different in nature does not mean being different from oneself. For he is not a nature; he has a nature.
Heretic: Let us grant that. What do you think, then? Is Christ not man? And is man not different from

Orthodox: Certainly.
Heretic: Then Christ is different from God.
Orthodox: But add the qualification "in his human nature," for in his divine nature he is not different.

Heretic: Then he is God and not God, which is a contradiction.
Orthodox: That is not a contradiction. He is not God and not God in the same respect, which is what would make it a contradiction. A human being is perceptible and not perceptible in different respects: perceptible in the body and not perceptible in the soul, and this is no contradiction. In just the same way, in truth, Christ is God and not God in different respects, and this is no contradiction. In respect of his Godhead he is God, but in respect of his humanity he is not God. So much for that.

Question of an Origenist to a believer. Abu Qurrah. Origenist.
Origenist: What justice is there in this: someone sins for ten or fifty years, and his punishment lasts for tens of thousands of ages, or rather for endless ages?
Abu Qurrah: And what is justice, according to you?
Origenist: That the punishment should be in proportion to the sin. That is, if someone has sinned for fifty years, he should be punished for the same number of fifty

Abu Qurrah: In how many ways do we learn what justice is? And where did you learn this justice of yours?
Origenist: You tell me: in how many ways?
Abu Qurrah: We know all justice from the law of God, or from laws laid down by men, or from the nature of things. None of these kinds of justice measures punishment by time. Take someone who commits fornication, or steals, or murders, in a single hour. When the law of God and the laws of men put the murderer to death and punish the lawbreaker, they do not punish him for a single hour. By putting him to death they [?] his punishment for all time. And you, if you caught someone committing adultery with your wife or your daughter, would you not judge that he should be punished not for one hour but handed over to death, which is an eternal punishment? The nature of things works the same way. Suppose we are warned against drinking cold water, say, or touching something harmful, and we disobey. We fall into a long-lasting punishment. Often, from drinking cold water, or touching fire, or taking vinegar, we have been punished with a lasting illness. And nature is perfectly just. But where do you get this justice of yours? Where did you find it?

Another dialogue of the same author with a Nestorian.
Abu Qurrah: Tell me, which nature does the name "Christ" indicate? The Godhead or the humanity?
Nestorian: Not one of them on its own, but the two hypostases, that is, God and the man together.
Abu Qurrah: Good. Tell me, then: was Christ born of a woman?
Nestorian: Yes.
Abu Qurrah: Then God the Word and the man were born of a woman, since Christ, as you have admitted, is God and the man. Again I ask you: did Christ die?
Nestorian: Yes.
Abu Qurrah: Then God and the man died. For according to you, Christ is God and the man.

Question: Is time in time, or not in time?
Answer: There are two ways to answer this. One is dialectical, from accepted opinion, and persuasive. The other is demonstrative, necessary, and true. But it must not be answered in a way that goes against accepted opinion.
Question: How, then, do you want the argument to proceed, dialectically or demonstratively?
Answer: Dialectically.
Question: Time is neither in time nor not in time. If it is not in time, it is separated from itself, which is impossible. If it is in time, it will be in itself. But what is in something is contained by it, and the thing contained is different from what contains it. So time would be different from itself, which is impossible. As has been shown, it is impossible for time to be separated from itself, and still more impossible for it to be different from itself. These results followed from supposing that time is either in time or not in time. So it is clear that time can be neither in time nor not in time, for every hypothesis that leads to something impossible is itself impossible. This has been argued dialectically and from accepted opinion. But if you also want me to argue demonstratively, I will not hesitate. Time is not in time, and we can be assured of this from similar cases. Place is not in a place, for everything in a place is a body, and place is not a body. The soul is not in a soul but in the body. Motion is not in motion but in what is moved. Colors are not in colors but in colored bodies. In the same way, time is not in time but in temporal things, and these are the things that are in motion, since time is the number of motion. So in the primary sense time is in motion. And since motion is in what is moved, time is also in what is moved, by way of motion. So it is true to say that time is not in time, but in motion or in what is moved: primarily in motion, and secondarily in what is moved, as has been said.

Another question by the same author. The Christian. The barbarian.
Barbarian: Whom do you say is the cause of good and

Barbarian: And whom do you say is the cause of evil?
Christian: That it comes from our own slackness and from the devil's wickedness.
Barbarian: Why is that?
Christian: Because of free will.
Barbarian: What, then? Are you free, so that you can do whatever you want, and do it?
Christian: In two things only. In other respects I was not made free by God.
Barbarian: What are these two things?
Christian: When I do good, I do not fear the law, but am honored and shown mercy by God. The devil too was made free by God, and he sinned, and God thrust him out of his own rank. But perhaps you will object: "What are good things and bad things? Look, the sun and the moon and the stars are good. Make one of them!" So I tell you that I do good and evil at the human level. Good things are such as glorifying God and prayer; bad things are fornication and theft. Now if, as you say, both good and evil come from God, then on your account God will be found unjust, which he is not. If God commanded, as you say, the fornicator to fornicate, the thief to steal, and the murderer to murder, then they deserve honor, because they did the will of God. And your lawgivers will be shown to be liars, and your books to be forgeries. For they command that the fornicator and the thief be flogged, even though they did the will of God, and that the murderer be put to death, when they ought to hon[or him]

The Saracen wanted to show that God is the cause of good and evil, and that God works together with the fornicator and the adulterer, so he said: "Who forms the infants in their mothers' wombs?"
Christian: Nowhere do I find Scripture saying that God formed or created anything after the first week. And you will never be able to prove that anything was created after that, except the rainbow, that is, the bow in the cloud in Noah's time. For [?]

having [?], he sowed seed in his own wife. So it is man who begets, as divine Scripture also says: "Adam begot Seth, and Seth begot Enosh, and Enosh begot Kenan." It did not say, "God formed Seth," or Enosh, or anyone else.

So Adam alone was formed by God, and the others are begotten and beget. In the same way the earth sprouts at God's command: "Let the earth bring forth green grass," it says. When the grass falls back onto the earth, or is sown by someone else, it sprouts. No one forms it; it obeys God's first command. So it is with me. As I said at the start, I am free in both good and evil. Wherever I sow, whether in my own wife or in another man's, I am using my own power, and the seed springs up and comes into being in obedience to God's first command, because what is sown has seminal power within itself. It is not that God is still forming and working day by day even now, since he made all things on the first day.
Saracen: Then how does God say to Jeremiah, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and from your mother I sanctified you"?
Christian: From Adam onward, God formed the ensouled seminal power of every man from the womb. Each man already has a son within his loins, and he begets him, and the son in turn begets another. The words "From the womb I sanctified you" have this meaning [?], as the Gospel says: "But to all who received him, who believe in his name, he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God," that is, through holy baptism.
Barbarian: And was there baptism before Christ? Jeremiah was born before Christ.
Christian: Yes, there was baptism, through the sea and the cloud: "For all were baptized into Moses." And if you ask, "How were those who lived before Moses baptized?" I will tell you that my Christ says, "Before Abraham was, I am." And again elsewhere, "For their sake I sanctify myself."

Barbarian: Do you call the one who does the will of God good or evil? If good, then you must also accept the Jews, since they did the will of your God, Christ, as you call him.
Christian: You say it was his will. I say it was his forbearance and patience. Listen to how. God said, "You shall not steal, you shall not commit fornication, you shall not murder." Did he say it so that we would steal and commit fornication and adultery and murder?
Barbarian: No. If he had wanted that, he would not have forbidden these things.
Christian: Good. You see, you have agreed with me that God does not want us to steal and commit fornication. If I get up right now and go and steal or murder, what do you call it? The will of God, or his forbearance and patience?
Barbarian: His forbearance and patience.
Christian: So it was with them. God was able to strike them down, but he let it pass. Whenever he wishes, if I do not repent, he repays me.
Barbarian: What do you say Christ is?
Christian: The Word of God, the Wisdom of God, the Son of God, the Arm of God, the Power, and countless other things. And what do you say Christ is?
Barbarian: I say Christ is the Spirit and Word of God.
Christian: And are these, the Spirit and the Word, uncreated or created?
Barbarian: Created.
Christian: Then who created the Word of God and the Spirit? Before God created them, what was God himself? Without Word and Spirit? Who would call God wordless, or without the Holy Spirit?
The barbarian fell silent.

Another question.
Are the words of the Lord created or uncreated? He put this question forward wanting to prove that the Word of God is created, which it is not. If you say they are created, he will tell you, "Created things are not called gods." If you say they are uncreated, he will tell you, "Look, all these, being words of God, are created and are not gods. And look, you admit that Christ, being the Word of God, is not God." So do not say they are created, or that they are uncreated. Say instead: "I confess only one Word of God, subsisting in his own hypostasis and uncreated. And I do not call the whole of my Scripture 'words,' but 'sayings.'"

Christian: The prophet spoke figuratively, and [?] literally.
Barbarian: And what are figurative speech and literal speech?
Christian: Literal speech is a firm demonstration of something; figurative speech is not a firm demonstration.
Barbarian: A prophet cannot say something that is not firm.

Christian: The prophets customarily give persons' traits to lifeless things. If you look, you will see them giving such things eyes and sight, as in "The sea saw and fled." But the sea has no eyes, since it is not a living thing. And again: "What ails you, O sea, that you fled?" and so on. And: "My sword shall devour flesh." Eating belongs to the mouth of someone who chews and drinks; a sword cuts, but it does not swallow. They also present rivers clapping their hands, hills leaping, and mountains skipping. In the same way, speaking figuratively, he called the sayings "words," when they are not words but

Another question.
Barbarian: The woman you call the Theotokos, did she die, or is she alive?
Christian: She did not die, and I say this relying on the proof of Scripture. The first man, for example, slept and had his rib taken from him. In the same way she committed her all-holy soul to God as if in sleep.
Barbarian: Look, I have been struck somewhere on my flesh. The flesh that was struck formed a welt, and in the welt a worm came into being. Who formed it?
Christian: We have said that after the first week of the world's making, we nowhere find God forming anything. He made all things that exist in six days, and then he was pleased that other things should come into being from those existing things, by his will alone. After the transgression the earth was condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles. So from then on our flesh too, being condemned, brings forth lice and worms.

Another question.
Saracen: In your view, who is greater, the one who sanctifies, or the one who

…the one being sanctified?" He asked this about the Baptist and Christ. Christian: "When you go to the bath with your slave, wanting to be washed by him, which do you call greater: that wretched slave, bought with silver, or yourself, who are cleansed by him?" The Saracen gave no answer to this.

By Abu Qurrah, to someone who asked him: "Since the ordinance [?] laid down for those under the Old [Testament] abstinence from unclean things and the eating of clean ones, how do those under the New recognize the eating of clean things and abstinence from unclean ones, when no law has taught them the difference? If they do this according to the tradition of the law, they ought to eat and abstain from everything the law proclaimed: eating sheep according to the law, but not eating camel or leopard. But if they are not enslaved to the law, how is it, again, that they abstain from what it forbade, such as horse, camel or mouse, or any of the unclean animals? As it is, since they neither obey the law wholly nor disobey it entirely, how can they avoid granting that each, I mean the law and grace, partly exercises its own nature and exhortation [?], and that by disobeying and obeying both they stand under law and grace, and again not under them?"

In the New Testament nothing that enters the mouth defiles a person. They abstain from what [others? ?] eat, not because the law prohibits it, but because it displeases the voluntary conscience of those who do not eat. Some, to achieve self-control, by their own choice abstain alike from clean and unclean foods, although they know that every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. Even so, we have reckoned thanksgiving for achieving self-control greater than thanksgiving for eating foods. For these reasons, then, law and grace have nothing in common, [not even] a part; the whole belongs to grace alone, both the eating and the abstaining from what is eaten, [as was said before? ?].

Another answer. By Arethas (70). Faith does not lie in foods, but in the settled… VARIANT READINGS: 87 ὑπ’ αὐτά, so that it refers to law and grace. 88 Read: [?]

…continuance in the faith. The use of foods is left to the custom of those who eat, as it was even before they became Christians. To the Jews, however, the distinction of foods was not given at random, but as a riddle showing how they ought to order the course of their life, drawing benefit from their diet. For example (to mention it briefly), the law forbade the Jews to eat hares and pigs, to show by this that, where it is pious to be manly, no trace of cowardice should cling to them, and that they should not lay claim to a sordid and loathsome life. So too with the other animals it forbade them to eat: they were to observe the natural peculiarity found in each and order the impulse of the soul in relation to it.

By the same Theodore, bishop of Harran, on Adam. By Photius. One must know that it is necessary to think and say that Adam's body was by nature mortal and subject to suffering, but by divine grace was kept immortal and free from suffering, until the transgression stripped it of the natural [grace? ?]. For so the choir of the saints declares.

What is death? And how is death put to death? [?] For the Church too glorifies [?]: "And behold, we die." Death is neither a substance nor does it subsist by itself; it is an affection that occurs in a substance, and its so-called being lasts only as long as it is occurring. Since death is predicated of several things and in different ways, one must know that death for an angel is the fall from heavenly and luminous glory, which Satan, being an angel, was the first to undergo. Death for the devil and a demon is the allotment to eternal fire at the last. Death for a human being is the separation of the soul from the body. Death of the soul is estrangement from God. And death to death is the firstfruits of our resurrection, which is Christ. Until him death served the corruption of human beings, and the hopelessness of resurrection was thought to be its life. But since Christ died and rose, its service has been turned to the opposite. For it no longer serves a corruption without hope, but a resurrection that is hoped for; and this is death for it. For that which puts to death is itself put to death by the hope of our resur- VARIANT READINGS: 83 τῆς ἐδωδῆς. 84 λεγομένην. 85 ὑπουργίας.

-rection. For whenever it sees a Christian dying in the hope of our resurrection, and the event being called sleep, it falls and is struck down by the stronger; and resurrection is stronger than death. So death has been put to death by the resurrection of Christ, and [by the deaths? ?] of Christians who die in the hope of resurrection. Thus death is always being put to death in part by this kind of service; but when the whole rises, following the firstfruits, then death too, as the Apostle says, having nothing left to serve, is abolished completely.

A concise teaching on the divine names, both those common to the Trinity and those proper to each person of the Trinity.

There are common names that extend through the Holy Trinity, being said of the divine essence: for example God, Lord, good, righteous, wise, powerful, King, Master, Creator, Provider, Savior, holy, and all such terms as are applied in common to the divine nature and do not belong peculiarly to one hypostasis. There are also proper names, that is, hypostatic ones: for example Father, Son, Holy Spirit. Of the common names said of the essence, "God" has been taken for the Father and has become as it were special to him, because he is the cause of the Son and the Spirit, and they are referred back to him. In the same way "Lord" has been taken for the Son, and "Holy Spirit" for the Spirit. Hence, whenever the apostles and nearly all of divine Scripture say "God" absolutely and without qualification, generally with the article and without any hypostatic property, they mean the Father. For example: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God," that is, of the Father. And again: "In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers," that is, the Father. And the creed of the faith: "[I believe] in one God," that is, the Father, "and in one Lord," that is, the Son. And the Apostle: "For even if there are many gods, yet for us there is one God, the Father." And: "Even if there are many lords, yet for us there is one Lord, the Son." "God" is said in a special sense because the union, that is, the unfolding and summing up of the Trinity, is the Fa- 1 Cor. 13:10.

…of God, arm of God, right hand of God. The Spirit likewise: Spirit of God, finger of God. So these are referred back to the Father himself, not the Father to them. And if you find the name "God" used of the Son, and "Lord" of the Father and of the Spirit, and "Holy" and "Spirit" of the Father (as in "Holy is God," clearly meaning the Father, and "God is Spirit"), these, being names of the nature, are sometimes predicated of the hypostases as well. So the Son too is called God predicatively, from the nature, and for the most part without the article, unless the discourse or phrase is already about him. In that case the article becomes a reference to him, as to a person already known, as in "from whom is the Christ according to the flesh," and "who is God over all."

One must also know this: none of the names indicates the essence of God, as names do with other things. If we say stone, or gold, or ox, or man, we indicate the essence of each by the name. But if we say God, or Lord, or King, or Father, or any name whatever of God, we signify an activity or a relation. "God" or "Maker" signifies an activity; "King," "Master" or "Father" signifies a relation.

On union and incarnation [?]. On union and incarnation: and that the person or hypostasis became incarnate, while the nature of the Godhead was united to human nature in the hypostasis of God the Word.

Incarnation is becoming human, and becoming human is the making of the one who became human into a man. And he who became human was made a man so that "man" might be predicated of him, and so that he who became human might receive both the name and the definition of man, as each human being does. The "man" that is predicated is the name of a nature, and it is a nature that is predicated of a hypostasis; nature is not predicated of nature. If, then, we confess this, it clearly holds in the same way that the hypostasis which became human, or the… …the subsistence became incarnate, while the divine nature was united to the human, in the person of God the Word.

…[eternal] Son. For the eternal Son, being perfect God, became man [without change? ?], and is at once perfect God and perfect man. The name "God" is predicated of him, as it is of the Father and of the Spirit, and again "man" is predicated of him, as of each of the rest of human beings. And the same Son is incarnate. The divine nature, however, is not said to be incarnate, because "man," that is, human nature, cannot be predicated of it. As we said before, nature is in no way predicated of nature, not in any manner whatever.

So the hypostasis of the eternal Son has become, to put it by way of illustration, like a torrent that receives two rivers. The torrent is said to receive both rivers, though neither river receives the other. In this way the eternal Son receives the name and the definition of God, while God in no way admits the name or the definition of man, nor does man admit the name or the definition of God. But the hypostasis of the eternal Son admits, without any deficiency, the name and the definition of both natures, I mean divinity and humanity. So even if the man is said to have been deified, he is not said to be deified in the sense that the man received the name and definition of God. If that were so, he would be consubstantial with the Father and the Spirit, just as the eternal Son, by becoming incarnate, became consubstantial with us. It is not easy even to invent such a thing, to say that the man is consubstantial with the Father and the Spirit. Besides, if that were so, the man himself would be the hypostasis; the divine nature would subsist in him and be moved by him, and the man would be the one moving the Godhead.

One must also know this: nothing is predicated absolutely of the divine nature that is not equally predicated of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For example, life, light, without beginning, unchangeable, and terms akin to these are predicated of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. If, then, incarnation were predicated of the divine nature, it would be predicated of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, just like the terms already mentioned. But this is full of every absurdity even when merely imagined in bare thought, let alone spoken: that is, to say that the Father and the Holy Spirit became incarnate. And if someone should say that everything predicated absolutely or properly of the hypostasis is also referred secondarily to the nature, and that since incarnation is predicated of the eternal Son, who is a hypostasis of the all-venerable Trinity, it should be referred secondarily from the hypostasis to the nature, let such a person know that whatever is referred secondarily from the hypostasis to the nature was present long before in the nature potentially [?],

and the hypostasis has inherited it from the nature in actuality. That is why such things are reasonably referred from the hypostasis to the nature: they pre-exist potentially in the nature but are found actually in the hypostasis. In the same way, the division into species, which exists potentially in the genus but actually in the species, is reasonably referred secondarily from the species to the genus. For example, "rational" is in "animal" potentially, but in "man" actually; and "animal" is called rational secondarily, because man is rational. Likewise, the particular differences that characterize the hypostasis of each human being are considered to be in "man" potentially, but are actually present in Socrates and Plato; and so they are referred from the hypostasis to the nature, or from Socrates to man. For example, we say that Socrates is hook-nosed or bald, and secondarily we say that man is likewise hook-nosed or bald because of Socrates, since, as we said, Socrates has inherited the hook nose and the baldness from man. But of the things that came together from the human lump into the hypostasis of God the Word through the hypostatic union, none at all was in the uncreated, incorporeal and impassible divine nature, either potentially or actually. For this reason the eternal [Son] is said to have become incarnate, to have been crucified and to have died, but the divine nature in no way, even though [it is in his hypostasis? ?].

If anyone blames himself for being slow to understand what has been said, and says that his mind cannot grasp how the divine nature, being in the hypostasis of the Son immovable and uncontainable, does not suffer with it when it suffers, and how, when something happens in the hypostasis, it is not said to have happened also in the nature, which is not separated from the hypostasis of the eternal Son, we will resolve the difficulty and bring him the quickest cure, drawing the proof from familiar things that are seen close at hand. You surely know, my friend, that each human being, Socrates, say, or Plato, is composed of an immaterial soul and a material body; and that the soul of Socrates is in him, and if it is separated from him Socrates cannot remain. Socrates is said to grow and to become large from small, to be cut or burned, while his soul undergoes none of these things, as is clear to all. In this way, then, advancing in the flesh and growing, and anything else human of this kind, is predicated of the eternal Son, while none of it attaches to the divine nature, just as it does not [to the soul] of Socrates. All the more, then, will none of the things predicated of the eternal Son in the flesh on account of the assumption be predicated of the pure nature. And just as, when we say that Socrates has been cut, we know that it is not Socrates' soul itself but his body that has been cut,

so, when we say that the eternal Son was wounded by the spear, we understand that the wound did not reach his divine [nature], which is incorruptible and indestructible, but his flesh, which could be wounded and cut.

We will also give you a solution to the difficulty from another quarter. Our mind, which is what perceives through the bodily eyes that see, also has another sight of its own, besides the sight that discerns through the eyes, and this we call contemplation. If, then, the body's power of sight should happen to be maimed, we do not say that the mind does not see, since its natural intellectual power of vision remains unaltered and [intact? ?]. So too the eternal Son is said to have suffered in the flesh, while his divine nature remained impassible. But why be led on by these examples, when this can be seen in the body, with its size and grossness? We all know that the mind sees through the eyes and hears through the ears; and the senses of sight and hearing, each distinct from the other, are seated in the brain, and the mind dwells with them. Although these are joined to one another and live together in one subject, it often happens that the bodily sight or hearing, or the mind itself, is harmed; yet the harm to one does not damage the rest, and their natural power is kept unharmed. Let us not be too astonished, then, if when the body of the eternal Son suffers, his indivisible [divine? ?] nature nonetheless remains impassible and unharmed, exalted above every essence, ruling over all, wholly incapable of suffering; with whom, according to the chief of the apostles, there is no change or shadow of turning.

I will also set before you [?] another example, in which you will be able to see as in a mirror how, if suffering or corruption befalls some hypostasis, it does not pass over to the nature, even if it happens [to have only one hypostasis? ?]. Suppose, my dear friend, you shape and fashion a statue from gold or bronze, and then melt it down again: the human likeness is lost and comes to nothing, but the gold or the bronze, which was the nature of the statue, remains unharmed and uncorrupted. But pay very close and sensible attention to the examples, and take care not to transfer to the divine doctrines everything that arises from them. Take only certain broad outlines and indications that lead toward contemplation, for the sake of which alone they are adopted, and only by analogy. Dismiss whatever is unfitting and unlike as far as possible, with a pious and steady mind, always separating the unlike from the like, like a most exact winnower winnowing the chaff from the grain.

The union of the two natures, I mean divinity and humanity, is said to have taken place in the hypostasis of the only-begotten, eternal Son of God without change, mixture or confusion, in this way. He was without beginning together with the Father and co-eternal with him, and in his own property had no other nature predicated of him besides the divine nature of the Father, uncreated and uncircumscribed. But through the abundance of his mercy and his ineffable love for humankind, for our salvation, in the last days he came down from heaven, which he did not leave in his all-filling Godhead. Becoming incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the all-blameless Ever-Virgin Mary, he had in himself, complete and undiminished, the created, passible and human essence, predicated of him just as the divine nature is. Since, then, the two natures came together in him and are predicated of him together, with all their natural properties, both are said to be united in each other in him, without change, confusion or alteration; for the two natures were united in one and the same hypostasis of the eternal Son. Hence the same eternal Son has been counted with the Father and the Spirit according to the divine nature, and the same is counted with us according to our human nature. In this respect the same Son, even after he became human and after the ineffable, unmixed and unconfused union of his two natures that came together, is one of humankind, not one thing and another. Through him we have been saved and called back to our ancient blessedness, made immortal and incorruptible through his saving sufferings, his life-giving death, his three-day burial and his resurrection from the dead. To him be glory, honor and might, with his Father, who is without beginning, and the all-holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
